Scope Management.q: A team identifies all the key deliverables that must be placed under version control. Which configuration management activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Scope Management.w: Configuration identification determines which items are to be controlled and labels them so they can be managed.

Scope Management.q: A client requests an urgent change to a critical deliverable. What should the project manager do first?
o: Implement the change straight away to meet expectations
Include the change within the next routine progress report
Email the project team and proceed with it immediately
Raise and assess a change request through the formal procedure
Scope Management.w: Every change, however urgent, is raised and assessed through the formal change control procedure so its impact is understood before any decision.

Scope Management.q: What is the role of configuration management once a scope change has been formally approved?
o: To carry out the approval of the original change request
To redefine the project's chosen life cycle for delivery
To ensure the approved change is applied and documented correctly
To communicate the approved change out to the stakeholders
Scope Management.w: After change control approves a change, configuration management ensures it is implemented, recorded and reflected in the controlled products.

Scope Management.q: Which configuration management activity ensures that only approved changes are made to configuration items?
o: Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Configuration control
Scope Management.w: Configuration control ensures that changes to controlled items follow the correct review and approval process before being made.

Scope Management.q: An audit confirms that versioning rules were followed and only approved changes were made. What does this outcome confirm?
o: That all of the planned benefits have been realised
That the stakeholder requirements have changed
That the agreed project baseline has since changed
That configuration control and verification were effective
Scope Management.w: A satisfactory audit demonstrates that changes were properly controlled and that items conform to their approved configuration.

Scope Management.q: An agile team reviews scope at the start of each sprint and updates priorities from user feedback. How does this reflect iterative scope management?
o: The deliverables are set upfront and reviewed only monthly
The product evolves through ongoing review and stakeholder input
The team proceeds without defining any scope at all
The scope is fixed at the start and is never revisited
Scope Management.w: In iterative projects the scope evolves as work progresses, guided by continual review and stakeholder feedback.

Scope Management.q: How do a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure support scope definition when used together?
o: They set out the project's risks and outstanding issues
They identify the communication channels and reporting lines
They link the deliverables to the work required to produce them
They record the financial transactions made for the stakeholders
Scope Management.w: Together the PBS and WBS connect what must be delivered to the work required to deliver it, giving a complete view of scope.

Scope Management.q: A project team uses the RACI model to assign responsibilities. Which type of tool are they using?
o: An organisational breakdown structure
A work breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) is a common form of responsibility assignment matrix used to clarify roles.

Scope Management.q: A senior stakeholder questions whether recent product updates were properly authorised. Which combination of processes evidences both approval and controlled implementation?
o: Change control and configuration management
Scheduling and stakeholder management
Benefits management and procurement
Risk management and issue tracking
Scope Management.w: Change control provides the record of approval, while configuration management shows the change was applied and tracked correctly.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes the role of a change control board on a project?
o: A group authorised to review and approve or reject scope changes
An external panel appointed to audit the project's accounts
A working group responsible for the project's external marketing
A team that decides on the project's team-building activities
Scope Management.w: A change control board is the body with the authority to evaluate change requests and decide whether to approve or reject them.

Scope Management.q: Midway through a project, a client requests several enhancements to the agreed product. What should the project manager do first?
o: Add the changes to the next sprint to save time
Notify finance to adjust the cost baseline
Submit a formal change request for review
Amend the configuration log directly
Update the WBS and proceed with changes
Scope Management.w: A formal change request must be submitted and reviewed before any changes are implemented to maintain scope control.

n.4: WBS should only be updated after a change is approved.
n.0: Unapproved changes can lead to misalignment and rework.
n.1: The cost baseline is adjusted only after the change is approved.
n.3: The configuration log is updated after the change is formally authorised.

Scope Management.q: A cost breakdown structure (CBS) most directly supports which of the following financial activities on a project?
o: Setting out the responsibilities held by each stakeholder
Assigning individual tasks to named members of the team
Estimating, budgeting and monitoring the project's costs
Monitoring the project's risks and its open issues
Scope Management.w: A CBS provides a structured breakdown of cost that underpins estimating, budgeting and ongoing cost monitoring for control.

Scope Management.q: A work breakdown structure contains items such as 'code user interface' and 'test module'. What does this structure help to define?
o: The procurement process for the external suppliers
The financial framework underpinning the project
The structure of the client's own organisation
The work required to produce each project deliverable
Scope Management.w: The WBS breaks the scope into the work required to complete each deliverable, expressed as manageable work packages.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between a PBS and a WBS?
o: The PBS defines the deliverables and the WBS defines the work to create them
The PBS defines the risks and the WBS defines the risk responses
The PBS sets the budget and the WBS sets the time limits
The PBS defines the costs and the WBS defines the people involved
Scope Management.w: The PBS identifies the product's deliverables, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes how a cost breakdown structure (CBS) supports effective budget control on a project?
o: By setting out the project's overall decision-making structure
By showing the cost associated with each part of the project
By categorising the project's scope into functional units
By assigning named individuals to each of the project tasks
Scope Management.w: By attributing costs to each project element, the CBS lets the project manager monitor and control spending against the budget.

Scope Management.q: Once a change has been implemented, what is a key final step in the change control process?
o: Monitor the impact and confirm alignment with project objectives
Notify the members of the wider supply chain
Archive all unused change request forms immediately
Submit the change again for a further round of approval
Scope Management.w: A post-implementation review confirms the change has delivered the intended benefit and remains aligned with the project's objectives without adverse side effects.

Scope Management.q: A review finds a project failed to deliver key elements because scope was poorly controlled. Which process should have prevented this?
o: Scope management
Resource scheduling
Communication planning
Risk analysis
Scope Management.w: Scope management ensures that all required deliverables are identified, defined and controlled throughout the project.

Scope Management.q: Why is change control generally less rigid in an iterative life cycle?
o: Because iterative projects avoid producing any documentation
Because scope is expected to evolve throughout delivery
Because testing takes place only at project closure
Because the project budget is fixed from the outset
Scope Management.w: Iterative life cycles anticipate that scope will be refined continuously, so change is handled more flexibly than in linear projects.

Scope Management.q: In configuration management, what does the term 'configuration item' typically refer to?
o: A stakeholder's preferred method of receiving communication
A deliverable or document that is placed under version control
A resource that has been assigned across several tasks
A task that lies on the project's overall critical path
Scope Management.w: A configuration item is any product, deliverable or document that is identified and controlled through the configuration management process.

Scope Management.q: A linear project finalised its scope during the concept phase. What is the likely consequence when new requirements emerge during delivery?
o: The change will be managed through strict change control
The scope will be re-planned freely at every stage
The change will be absorbed into the work automatically
The team will simply reprioritise its next sprint
Scope Management.w: Linear projects fix scope early, so new requirements arising later are handled through a formal, strictly controlled change process.

Scope Management.q: After a change, the team confirms that the new deliverable matches the approved configuration. Which activity is this?
o: Configuration planning
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration identification
Scope Management.w: Verification and audit confirm that items conform to their approved configuration and that changes were made correctly.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder asks whether the latest test script represents the most current version. Which configuration activity provides the answer?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Status accounting records the version history, current status and location of each controlled item, allowing such questions to be answered.

Scope Management.q: In a linear project with scope locked at the concept phase, a client requests a significant change during delivery. How is this typically handled?
o: It is implemented without review to avoid delay
It is added straight into the next delivery sprint
It is deferred until the benefits realisation phase
It is assessed through a formal change control process
Scope Management.w: Linear projects manage changes to a fixed scope through a formal change control process to maintain control of the project.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is not normally an activity within the configuration management process?
o: Status accounting
Configuration procurement
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Procurement is not part of configuration management; the recognised activities include planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of scope management in a linear project?
o: Frequent reprioritisation of user stories each cycle
Continuous negotiation of scope with the stakeholders
Formal control of changes once the initial scope is defined
Dynamic delivery of requirements as they evolve
Scope Management.w: Linear projects define scope early and rely on formal change control to evaluate and manage any changes thereafter.

Scope Management.q: A project sets up a version-controlled folder with controlled access for all configuration items. Which activity does this address?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration control
Scope Management.w: Configuration control includes the procedures that govern controlled access and the storage of approved item versions.

Scope Management.q: A developer implements a software change from an informal request, and it later proves incompatible with existing modules. Which process breakdown occurred?
o: Stakeholder mapping was not kept properly up to date
Change control was bypassed and configuration was not enforced
Quality control was applied too heavily to the work
Risk escalation was skipped during the delivery phase
Scope Management.w: The change was not authorised through change control and was not verified or integrated through configuration management, so both controls failed.

Scope Management.q: A team has implemented a change, but its effects on cost and schedule were never recorded. Which change control step was most likely omitted?
o: Approval by the project sponsor
Impact assessment
Configuration verification audit
Change request logging
Scope Management.w: Impact assessment identifies the cost, time, quality and risk effects of a change and must precede approval and implementation.

Scope Management.q: A project manager notices discrepancies between the latest deliverable and the configuration baseline. Which process should be reviewed first?
o: Procurement management
Scheduling control
Communication planning
Configuration management
Scope Management.w: Configuration management keeps deliverables aligned with the current approved baseline, so it should be reviewed when discrepancies appear.

Scope Management.q: While reviewing the configuration log, a project support officer finds two conflicting versions of a technical specification. Which configuration process has most likely failed?
o: Resource levelling
Risk mitigation
Benefits tracking
Version control
Scope Management.w: Version control ensures a single current, approved version is in use, so conflicting versions point to a failure of this control.

Scope Management.q: Which process ensures that a project delivers only the work required to meet its objectives?
o: Cost management
Change control
Stakeholder management
Scope management
Scope Management.w: Scope management defines and controls the work included in the project so that it delivers only what is necessary to meet its objectives.

Scope Management.q: A project manager creates an organisational breakdown structure (OBS). What is the main purpose of this tool?
o: To record the project's detailed work breakdown structure
To show the reporting relationships and lines of authority
To define the project's risks and their planned responses
To set out the methods used to communicate with stakeholders
Scope Management.w: An OBS sets out the project's organisational hierarchy, showing roles, reporting relationships and lines of authority.

Scope Management.q: A project board rejects a change after assessment shows high cost for limited benefit. What does this demonstrate about change control?
o: It speeds up delivery through early implementation
It removes the need for any stakeholder input
It ensures that only beneficial changes are implemented
It supports uncontrolled changes to the project scope
Scope Management.w: Change control applies formal evaluation so the project is protected from changes that are unnecessary or harmful to its objectives.

Scope Management.q: What is the primary purpose of change control within project scope management?
o: To adjust the project's budget in line with the latest forecasts
To allow changes to proceed without approval to maintain momentum
To develop the initial scope statement at the start of the project
To assess and then approve or reject proposed changes to scope
Scope Management.w: Change control is the formal process for assessing proposed changes and deciding whether to approve or reject them before implementation.

Scope Management.q: A team uses a work breakdown structure to define tasks and a product breakdown structure to define deliverables. What is a key benefit of using both?
o: They remove the need to maintain a stakeholder register
They reduce the need for a procurement process
They provide a legal framework for engaging suppliers
They link the work required to the outputs that are expected
Scope Management.w: Using both structures ensures the planned work is directly connected to the agreed outputs the project must deliver.

Scope Management.q: A project manager uses a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM). What is the key benefit of using this tool?
o: It tracks the financial cost incurred against each project phase
It allocates the packages of work to their related deliverables
It shows who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed
It breaks the project schedule down into its individual tasks
Scope Management.w: A RAM, often using RACI, maps who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task, giving clear role accountability.

Scope Management.q: Why are both change control and configuration management needed together in scope management?
o: To evaluate and approve changes and then maintain them in the outputs
To prevent any changes at all from being made to the project
To provide the project's budget approval and procurement sign-off
To handle only the external modifications made to contracts
Scope Management.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures those approved changes are correctly applied and maintained.

Scope Management.q: Which document typically captures the details of a proposed scope change before it is formally reviewed?
o: Change request form
Stakeholder matrix
Configuration item log
Communication plan
Scope Management.w: A change request form initiates the process, recording the proposed change and its rationale so it can be assessed and a decision made.

Scope Management.q: Why must configuration management and change control operate together on a project?
o: To assign the members of the team to their delivery roles
To allow the project to eliminate the use of baselines
To ensure changes are properly evaluated, approved and implemented
To remove the need for any formal documentation of change
Scope Management.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures they are consistently applied and documented.

Scope Management.q: Which process ensures that changes to scope are formally approved so they do not adversely affect quality or budget?
o: Risk escalation
Resource allocation
Team briefing
Change control
Scope Management.w: Change control assesses, authorises and integrates proposed changes so the impact on quality, cost and time is controlled.

Scope Management.q: A senior stakeholder wants to understand how reporting will work across the project's several teams. Which structure should the project manager refer them to?
o: The product breakdown structure (PBS)
The organisational breakdown structure (OBS)
The work breakdown structure (WBS)
The cost breakdown structure (CBS)
Scope Management.w: The OBS shows reporting lines and how roles fit within the project's organisation, which is exactly what the stakeholder is asking about.

Scope Management.q: When is a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) most useful during a project?
o: When defining the project's overall scope and its schedule
When conducting the project's lessons learned review at closure
When assigning clear ownership of deliverables and decision-making
When establishing the communication channels with stakeholders
Scope Management.w: The RAM is most valuable when ownership and accountability for deliverables and decisions must be made explicit.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is true of a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM)?
o: It defines the physical components of the final product
It determines the order of the project's activities
It links organisational roles to the project's tasks
It sets the level of influence held by each stakeholder
Scope Management.w: A RAM matches roles from the OBS to the tasks in the WBS, ensuring each activity has clearly assigned responsibility.

Scope Management.q: A team uses a product breakdown structure (PBS) to represent the end product. What is its primary purpose in scope management?
o: To allocate costs to individual project activities
To estimate the overall schedule for the project
To define the deliverables that make up the final product
To assign team members to each project task
Scope Management.w: A PBS breaks the end product down hierarchically to define the deliverables that make up the final product.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is developing a cost breakdown structure (CBS) for a project. What is the main purpose of this structure?
o: To record the issues and lessons learned during delivery
To break the deliverables down into manageable packages of work
To set out the reporting lines that exist between team members
To identify and track the costs of the project's individual components
Scope Management.w: A CBS breaks the project's costs down against its components, giving the project manager a structured basis for budgeting and cost control.

Scope Management.q: Why might a project manager create a product breakdown structure before a work breakdown structure?
o: To create a baseline budget for the project
To determine the cost of the individual tasks first
To assign team members to their roles early on
To establish a shared understanding of the product to be delivered
Scope Management.w: The PBS clarifies the deliverables required, giving a shared understanding of the product so that the WBS can be built around it.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor wants the flexibility to refine requirements as user needs emerge. Which life cycle is better suited, and why?
o: Linear, because it freezes the scope right from the start
Iterative, because it removes the need for any planning
Iterative, because it supports evolving scope through continuous feedback
Linear, because it copes best with high levels of uncertainty
Scope Management.w: An iterative life cycle is designed to accommodate changing requirements, allowing scope to evolve through continuous feedback.

Scope Management.q: How does an organisational breakdown structure (OBS) support role clarity within a project team?
o: By setting out the project's configuration control procedures
By identifying the deliverables that the project must produce
By showing how responsibilities are distributed through the organisation
By detailing the project's individual financial cost centres
Scope Management.w: The OBS clarifies who holds responsibility and who reports to whom, improving transparency of roles across the team.

Scope Management.q: A configuration log records the current status of each controlled item. Which configuration management activity does this represent?
o: Status accounting
Configuration control
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Status accounting keeps a traceable record of the status of every configuration item and the changes made to it.

Scope Management.q: A proposed change is rejected because it would create inconsistencies with existing components. Which process supported this decision?
o: Risk assessment
Schedule management
Quality assurance
Configuration management
Scope Management.w: Configuration management maintains the integrity and consistency of the product, so it can identify a change that would conflict with existing items.

Scope Management.q: A product breakdown structure sets out the main product, its subassemblies and its components. Why is this useful to the project manager?
o: It identifies which work packages are behind schedule
It clarifies exactly what the project must deliver
It shows who is responsible for each delivery
It allocates team members to each activity
Scope Management.w: The PBS defines and visualises all elements of the final product, clarifying exactly what the project must deliver.

Scope Management.q: A client requests a change to a configured product, and it must be assessed and approved before work begins. Which process provides this formal evaluation?
o: Stakeholder engagement
Risk management
Change control
Scope definition
Scope Management.w: Change control provides the formal route for assessing and approving or rejecting a change before it affects any configuration items.

Scope Management.q: Why is a post-implementation review an essential part of the change control process?
o: To ensure the change was recorded within the supplier contract
To validate that all stakeholders were formally consulted first
To confirm the change achieved its intended outcomes without adverse effects
To determine the payment terms owed to the supplier
Scope Management.w: The review confirms the change was effective and has not introduced new problems in other areas of the project.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following statements best describes the function of an organisational breakdown structure (OBS)?
o: It sets out the required packages of work in a hierarchy
It assigns a specific cost to each member of the team
It shows the structure of roles and reporting within the project
It defines the sequence in which tasks are to be delivered
Scope Management.w: An OBS is a hierarchical view of how the project is organised, showing roles and who reports to whom.

Scope Management.q: What does configuration management rely on to determine whether a proposed update can be safely implemented?
o: Approval given through the change control process
The project's overall work breakdown structure
The procedures used for escalating project risks
The project's stakeholder map and analysis
Scope Management.w: Configuration management only applies changes that have first been formally assessed and approved through change control.

Scope Management.q: How does a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) help to reduce duplication of effort on a project?
o: By ranking the project's activities in their order of criticality
By defining the communication channels between the stakeholders
By assigning each member of the team to a specific budget code
By clarifying who is responsible and accountable for each task
Scope Management.w: By assigning clear responsibility and accountability, the RAM prevents overlap and confusion about who should do each task.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor asks for proof that recent product updates match the approved changes. Which configuration management records should be provided?
o: The version history and the configuration log
The stakeholder matrix and the project's RAID log
The updated work and organisational breakdown structures
The lessons learned report and the project audit plan
Scope Management.w: Version histories and the configuration log evidence that approved changes were tracked and correctly implemented in the product.

Scope Management.q: During testing a stakeholder suggests altering the interface, and the team updates the prototype without formal approval. What risk does this pose?
o: It reduces the project's reliance on captured lessons learned
It improves team morale but delays the realisation of benefits
It helps the team to finalise the configuration log early
It may cause scope creep and misalignment with the baseline
Scope Management.w: Changing a product without change control means the impact is not assessed, risking scope creep and divergence from the agreed baseline.

Scope Management.q: What does version control help to ensure within the configuration management process?
o: That outdated documents are clearly identified and replaced
That the project's tasks are placed in the correct sequence
That the project's procurement rules are properly followed
That the entries in the risk register are correctly prioritised
Scope Management.w: Version control ensures that only the latest approved versions of documents and products are in use, and older versions are withdrawn.

Scope Management.q: What is the main difference between a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure?
o: The PBS shows the deliverables and the WBS shows the work to create them
The PBS sets the deadlines and the WBS sets the budgets
The PBS shows the work and the WBS shows the associated costs
The PBS supports communication and the WBS supports risk management
Scope Management.w: The PBS defines what the project must produce, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

Scope Management.q: An agile team adapts its backlog regularly throughout delivery. What does this indicate about scope management on the project?
o: Scope is left undefined until testing begins
Scope is adapted continuously as the project evolves
Scope is fixed and unchanged after the concept phase
Scope is fully defined at the start and then locked
Scope Management.w: Regular backlog refinement reflects iterative scope management, in which scope adapts to evolving priorities and feedback.

Scope Management.q: What must happen before a change can be applied to a project's baseline?
o: Declaration of a change freeze across the project
Renegotiation of the relevant supplier contract
Deletion of the affected configuration item
Formal approval through the change control process
Scope Management.w: No change should be applied to a baseline until it has been formally assessed and approved through change control.

Scope Management.q: Which configuration management activity defines how items will be controlled and versioned throughout a project?
o: Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Scope Management.w: Configuration planning sets out the framework, roles and procedures for how configuration items will be managed across the project.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best explains the distinction between change control and configuration management?
o: Change control evaluates proposed changes, and configuration management ensures approved changes are correctly implemented
Change control tracks scheduling milestones, and configuration management carries out product testing
Change control plans the use of resources, and configuration management defines the project team's roles
Change control manages procurement, and configuration management handles the project's budget reporting
Scope Management.w: Change control is the gatekeeper that assesses and approves changes; configuration management ensures approved changes are applied and maintained.

Scope Management.q: How does a cost breakdown structure (CBS) help a project manager with tracking project costs?
o: By allocating a named team member to each individual task
By linking a cost to each element of the project's scope
By listing the decision gates set throughout the project
By recording the lessons learned from earlier projects
Scope Management.w: The CBS links costs to defined elements of scope, allowing the project manager to track actual spending against the budget.

Scope Management.q: A linear project fixes all deliverables before work starts, while an iterative project adapts them over time. What does this show about scope management?
o: Iterative projects carry out no planning before delivery
Linear projects are inherently less reliable than iterative ones
Iterative projects manage scope incrementally as understanding grows
Iterative projects fail to define their scope at all
Scope Management.w: Iterative projects manage scope in increments, refining it as understanding of the requirements improves.

Scope Management.q: Testing reveals a flaw and the team wants to modify a deliverable. Which process ensures the change is formally evaluated and approved?
o: Risk assessment
Benefits management
Change control
Schedule control
Scope Management.w: Change control ensures any alteration to scope or a deliverable is formally reviewed and authorised before it is implemented.

Scope Management.q: A supplier requests a change to a component because of a manufacturing constraint, so the project manager raises a change request. Which process decides whether the change is accepted?
o: Change control
Scheduling optimisation
Risk escalation
Scope definition
Scope Management.w: Change control is the formal process used to evaluate a change request and decide whether the change to scope should be accepted.

Scope Management.q: Which statement best describes how scope is managed differently in linear and iterative projects?
o: Linear projects fix scope early, whereas iterative projects adapt it over time
Linear projects define scope late, whereas iterative projects define it early
Both linear and iterative projects fix their scope only at project closure
Iterative projects rely on strict change control, whereas linear projects stay flexible
Scope Management.w: Linear projects establish scope early in the life cycle, whereas iterative projects refine it throughout delivery.

Scope Management.q: A developer implements a change to a deliverable before it has been reviewed or authorised. Which stage of the change control process has been omitted?
o: Post-implementation review
Benefits review
Configuration audit
Impact assessment
Scope Management.w: Impact assessment evaluates the effect of a proposed change on time, cost, quality and risk before it can be approved and implemented.

Scope Management.q: A developer works from an outdated version of a requirements document. Which configuration management activity has failed?
o: Verification audit
Status accounting
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Status accounting maintains and communicates the current status of items; when it fails, out-of-date versions are used in error.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best explains how a product breakdown structure supports scope definition?
o: It lists all stakeholders and their communication preferences
It defines the product deliverables in a structured hierarchy
It records the planned and actual cost of each activity
It organises the reporting structure of the project team
Scope Management.w: The PBS sets out the product's deliverables in a structured hierarchy, giving a clear understanding of the required scope.

Scope Management.q: A deliverable is altered without going through the change control process. What is the most likely outcome?
o: More efficient approval of the change by the control board
Reduced cost and improved satisfaction among stakeholders
Stronger compliance with the project's quality standards
Increased risk of scope creep and unplanned rework
Scope Management.w: Unauthorised changes bypass assessment of their impact, leading to scope creep, misalignment with the baseline and likely rework.

Scope Management.q: A configuration audit finds that several different versions of the same document are in active use. Which activity has failed?
o: Configuration identification
Configuration control
Verification audit
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Configuration control should prevent unauthorised or duplicate versions from being released and used across the project.

Scope Management.q: An IT team delivers in two-week sprints, and the client requests changes after each review. What does this indicate about scope?
o: Scope is tightly fixed at the beginning of the project
Scope is determined only at the close of the project
Scope is evolving continuously through collaboration
Scope is restricted to the original deliverables only
Scope Management.w: This is iterative scope management, in which requirements evolve through continuous collaboration, review and feedback.

Scope Management.q: Which sequence best represents the typical flow of a change control process?
o: Approve, escalate, configure, then define
Assess, approve, implement, then review
Implement, review, approve, then log
Reject, implement, report, then close
Scope Management.w: A change is first assessed for impact, then formally approved, implemented in a controlled way, and finally reviewed to confirm the outcome.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best defines configuration management in the context of a project?
o: Measuring the project's performance against its agreed baselines
Planning the allocation of resources across the packages of work
Estimating the level of budget reserve the project should hold
Identifying, controlling and tracking the project's products and their changes
Scope Management.w: Configuration management is the technical and administrative activity of identifying, controlling, accounting for and verifying a project's products throughout their life.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder submits a formal request to alter a key deliverable. What is the first step in the change control process?
o: Escalate the matter straight to the project board
Implement the requested change to the deliverable immediately
Log the change request and assess its likely impact
Update the configuration baseline before any review
Scope Management.w: The first stage of change control is to log the request and assess its impact on time, cost, quality and risk before any decision.

Scope Management.q: In which phase of a typical linear life cycle is the project scope first defined and documented?
o: The delivery phase
The handover phase
The concept phase
The benefits realisation phase
Scope Management.w: The concept phase establishes the early definition of scope as part of the initial planning of the project.

Scope Management.q: A configuration management plan is produced during initiation. What does this plan typically include?
o: A list of the approved external procurement providers
Roles, responsibilities, item tracking methods and audit schedules
The benefits realisation strategy for the whole project
A detailed cost breakdown of each individual task
Scope Management.w: The configuration plan defines the framework for managing items, including who is responsible, how items are tracked, and when audits occur.

Scope Management.q: Why is a cost breakdown structure (CBS) usually derived from the work breakdown structure (WBS) on a project?
o: Because the WBS identifies the work that then needs to be costed
Because the CBS defines the thresholds for approving scope change
Because the WBS controls how stakeholders are communicated with
Because the CBS sets the reporting line for each work package
Scope Management.w: The WBS defines the work to be done, and the CBS attributes cost estimates to those components, so the two structures align.

Scope Management.q: A work breakdown structure is being developed for a software deployment project. What level of detail should it provide?
o: A breakdown of all the work packages needed to complete the deliverables
The roles and responsibilities of each team member
Only the financial costs linked to each task
Only the task names together with their durations
Scope Management.w: The WBS should decompose the total scope into smaller, manageable work packages that capture all the work required.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager revises the likelihood rating of an existing risk after new information arrives. Where is this recorded?
o: In the project issue log
In the stakeholder register
In the risk register
In the schedule baseline
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk register is kept up to date throughout the project to reflect changes in likelihood, impact and status.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A key risk recorded in the project's risk register has now materialised. What should happen next?
o: It should be ignored because it has already been analysed
It should be closed and recorded as a completed milestone
It should be deleted from the risk register without further action
It should be reclassified as an issue and managed accordingly
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once a risk actually occurs it becomes a current problem, so it is reclassified as an issue and handled through the issue management process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A stakeholder raises a formal complaint during a project review meeting. Which process is used to handle this?
o: Scope management
Risk identification
Configuration management
Issue management
Risk & Issue Management.w: A complaint is a current concern that has arisen, so it is captured and addressed through the issue management process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A software defect has been fixed, tested and verified. What is the final step in the issue resolution process?
o: Escalation of the issue to a higher authority
Closure of the issue, recording it as complete
Reassessment of the issue's potential impact
Reopening the issue for further investigation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once an issue has been resolved and verified, it is formally closed and recorded as complete.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does effective risk management benefit a project?
o: It shifts every decision onto the individual team members
It reduces the impact of threats and helps exploit opportunities
It removes all uncertainty from the project environment
It allows the project to ignore its business case
Risk & Issue Management.w: Managing risk reduces the effect of threats and helps the project take advantage of opportunities, improving the chance of success.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team decides to take no pre-emptive action against a possible delay to key components. Which risk response is this?
o: Transfer
Acceptance
Avoidance
Mitigation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Acceptance means acknowledging a risk and taking no pre-emptive action unless it actually materialises.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement best defines a 'risk' in the context of project management?
o: A confirmed problem that requires immediate resolution by the team
An uncertain event that, should it occur, would affect the project's objectives
A completed task that is currently waiting for formal approval
A cost overrun that has already occurred and cannot be recovered
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is an uncertain future event that may have a positive or negative effect on project objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best illustrates a risk on a project?
o: The project sponsor has already resigned from their post
A key supplier has already defaulted on an agreed delivery
The team has already exceeded the budget agreed for the phase
Adverse weather could delay the construction work later in the year
Risk & Issue Management.w: Adverse weather is an uncertain future event that may delay delivery, so it is a risk; the others have already happened and are issues.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager arranges a backup supplier agreement in case the main vendor fails to deliver. Which risk response is this?
o: Risk acceptance
Risk transfer
Contingency planning
Risk avoidance
Risk & Issue Management.w: Preparing a fallback to be used only if the risk occurs is a contingency (fallback) response.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk plan notes that poor weather may delay construction. What benefit does identifying this early provide?
o: It removes the impact of every environmental risk on the project
It gives the team time to prepare responses before any delay occurs
It removes the need for configuration control during the project
It guarantees that the project will remain within its agreed scope
Risk & Issue Management.w: Identifying risks early is the purpose of risk management: it allows responses to be planned before problems arise.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the main purpose of risk management on a project?
o: To improve the chance of meeting objectives by managing uncertainty
To replace the need for a project management plan
To transfer all responsibility for the project to the sponsor
To eliminate every possible risk before the project begins
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management aims to increase the likelihood of achieving objectives by identifying and responding to uncertainty, not to remove all risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the primary purpose of the risk identification stage?
o: To capture and record potential future events that may affect objectives
To assign risk owners and set aside their mitigation budgets
To resolve every open issue before project execution begins
To remove all uncertainty from the project management plan
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk identification focuses on uncovering and recording potential future events that could affect the project's objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The development team reports a defect that is preventing key features from working. How should this be treated?
o: As an issue, because it is already affecting the project
As a change request, because the scope has altered
As a constraint, because it limits the design
As a risk, because it may affect the project later
Risk & Issue Management.w: A defect that is actively preventing features from working has already occurred, so it is an issue that must be managed and resolved.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does a 'risk' differ from a 'certainty' in project management terms?
o: A risk lies outside the manager's control, whereas a certainty does not
A risk concerns team behaviour, whereas a certainty concerns the sponsor
A risk involves uncertainty, whereas a certainty does not
A risk always leads to failure, whereas a certainty leads to success
Risk & Issue Management.w: The defining feature of a risk is uncertainty: it may or may not occur, unlike a certainty.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team colour-codes its risks red, amber and green to show their severity. What is this an example of?
o: Qualitative risk analysis
Quantitative risk analysis
Configuration management
Critical path analysis
Risk & Issue Management.w: Ranking risks by descriptive categories such as red, amber and green is a form of qualitative risk analysis.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team recognises that a supplier might fail to meet its deadlines. Which stage of risk management does this demonstrate?
o: Risk identification
Risk acceptance
Risk avoidance
Risk exploitation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Spotting a potential future threat before it materialises is an example of risk identification.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best defines a project issue?
o: A problem that has already occurred and requires resolution
A possible delay that could arise during execution
An uncertain event that may affect the project in future
A threat for which a mitigation strategy must be planned
Risk & Issue Management.w: In APM terms an issue is an event that has already happened, or is happening now, and must be resolved, unlike a risk which is an uncertain future event.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement best describes the difference in timing between an issue and a risk?
o: An issue is a future possibility, whereas a risk is a current event
An issue is a current or past event, whereas a risk is a future possibility
Both an issue and a risk describe events that may occur in future
Both an issue and a risk describe events that have already occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is a present or past event requiring resolution, while a risk is an uncertain event that has not yet occurred.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier misses a key delivery, so the project manager records it and assigns it to the procurement lead. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Analysis of the issue's impact on objectives
Identification and assignment of the issue
Closure of the issue once it is verified
Resolution of the issue through corrective action
Risk & Issue Management.w: Logging the issue and giving it an owner are part of the initial identification and assignment stage of the resolution process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard step in the issue resolution process?
o: Analysis
Closure
Rescheduling
Identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: Rescheduling may be a consequence of resolving an issue but is not itself a formal step in the issue resolution process, which runs from identification to closure.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier fails to deliver components on time, delaying the schedule. What is the role of issue management in this situation?
o: To revise the scope so the affected tasks are removed
To document the issue, assign ownership and track its resolution
To plan the resources needed for the next project phase
To reassess the project's future risks and update tolerances
Risk & Issue Management.w: Issue management handles real disruptions such as a missed delivery by logging them, assigning an owner and tracking them through to resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following would you NOT normally expect to find recorded in a risk register?
o: The actual durations recorded for completed project tasks
A clear description of each identified risk
The probability and impact scores for each risk
The named person who owns each identified risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: Actual task durations belong to the schedule, not the risk register, which focuses on uncertainty and responses.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the primary purpose of a risk register in project management?
o: To record and manage identified risks and their planned responses
To record the availability of staff across the project
To maintain the project's formal change control log
To monitor the day-to-day tasks of the project team
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk register is the tool used to document identified risks, their status and their planned responses.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team holds a brainstorming session to work out what could prevent successful delivery. Which risk management stage is this?
o: Risk analysis
Risk response
Risk closure
Risk identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: Brainstorming is a common technique used during risk identification to surface possible risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best describes the escalation step in the issue resolution process?
o: Recording the lessons learned after the issue is resolved
Logging the issue formally when it is first identified
Raising the issue beyond project authority for a decision
Assigning the issue to a stakeholder for resolution
Risk & Issue Management.w: Escalation is used when an issue exceeds the project manager's authority and requires a decision from a higher level of governance.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project passes a risky component to a specialist third party under contract. Which risk response is being used?
o: Acceptance
Mitigation
Transfer
Avoidance
Risk & Issue Management.w: Transfer shifts responsibility for a risk to another party, commonly through a contract or insurance.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement correctly describes a project issue?
o: It is an uncertainty relating to the project business case
It is an unplanned event that has occurred and needs management attention
It is a scheduled event that is recorded in the risk register
It is a constraint that has been imposed by the project sponsor
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is an actual, unplanned event affecting the project that requires management action to resolve it.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the primary purpose of issue management within a project?
o: To develop contingency plans for anticipated external risks
To estimate the overall duration of the project's activities
To record, evaluate and resolve events that have already occurred
To identify and assess possible future threats to the project
Risk & Issue Management.w: Issue management provides a structured approach to capturing, assessing and resolving events that have already happened during the project.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the purpose of producing a risk response plan?
o: To document the acceptance criteria for the project's final deliverables
To define how the team will react once issues have been logged
To develop the project's work breakdown structure
To set out the actions that will reduce, avoid, transfer or accept each risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk response plan records the agreed action for each risk, whether to reduce, avoid, transfer or accept it.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best defines an 'issue' in a project?
o: An uncertain event that may or may not happen in future
A technique used to break down the scope of the work
A problem that has occurred and requires management action
A planned milestone marking the end of a project stage
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is a problem that has already happened and needs resolving now, unlike a risk, which is an uncertain future event.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is typically carried out during the resolution step of the issue management process?
o: Assigning the issue to a responsible team member
Determining the overall severity of the issue
Recording the issue formally in the register
Taking corrective action to resolve the issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: The resolution step involves implementing the planned corrective action to deal with and close out the issue.

Risk & Issue Management.q: When should a project risk normally be formally closed?
o: At the very start of the project's initiation stage
When it is no longer relevant or has been fully addressed
Only after the post-project review has taken place
As soon as it has first been identified by the team
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is closed once it no longer poses a threat or opportunity, whether through response or expiry.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is typically recorded during the closure stage of issue resolution?
o: The stakeholder responsibility matrix for the project
The proposed escalation route for the issue
The date the issue was resolved and the actions taken
The estimated likelihood of the issue recurring later
Risk & Issue Management.w: At closure the resolution date and a summary of the actions taken are recorded to confirm the issue is complete.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team uses a probability and impact matrix to assess its risks. What are they doing?
o: Creating the risk register
Performing risk analysis
Prioritising the lessons learned
Carrying out risk identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: A probability and impact matrix is a standard method of carrying out qualitative risk analysis.

Risk & Issue Management.q: In quantitative risk analysis, which technique might a team use to simulate many possible risk outcomes?
o: The Delphi technique
MoSCoW prioritisation
An Ishikawa diagram
Monte Carlo simulation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Monte Carlo simulation is a quantitative technique that models many scenarios to estimate the range of likely outcomes.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team recognises potential cyber-attacks as a threat to delivery. What has this activity achieved?
o: It has identified a risk
It has closed the risk
It has analysed the risk's impact
It has accepted the risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: Recognising cyber-attacks as a possible future threat means the team has successfully identified a risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A high-impact, low-probability risk has been identified. What should risk analysis then help the team decide?
o: Whether to accept, avoid, reduce or transfer it as the response
Whether to delay the whole project until the threat has passed
Whether to ignore the risk simply because it is unlikely to occur
Whether to remove the affected deliverable from the project
Risk & Issue Management.w: Analysis of likelihood and impact informs the choice of an appropriate response, such as accept, avoid, reduce or transfer.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier has failed to deliver a critical component, halting project work. How should this be classified?
o: An issue, because the problem has already occurred
A milestone, because it marks a point in the schedule
An assumption, because it was expected during planning
A risk, because it might affect the project later
Risk & Issue Management.w: A problem that has already happened and is affecting the project is an issue, not a risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project's main server crashes, halting all progress. How should this event most accurately be classified?
o: As a risk, because it may affect the schedule
As a constraint, because it limits progress
As a milestone, because it marks an event
As an issue, because it has already occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: The crash has already happened and is affecting delivery, so it is an issue to be managed and resolved rather than an uncertain future risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During which stage of the issue resolution process is the effect of the issue on project objectives determined?
o: Closure
Analysis
Resolution
Identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: The analysis stage examines the severity and implications of the issue for the project's objectives before deciding how to address it.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best describes the difference between an issue and a risk?
o: A risk relates to cost, whereas an issue relates to quality
A risk must be escalated, whereas an issue does not
A risk is recorded in the schedule, whereas an issue is not
A risk is a future uncertainty, whereas an issue is a current problem
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is an uncertain future event, while an issue is a problem that has already occurred and must be resolved.

Risk & Issue Management.q: An issue has occurred within a project. Which process is used to resolve it?
o: Configuration management
Change control
Issue management
Risk management
Risk & Issue Management.w: Issue management is the structured process for recording, assessing and resolving problems once they have occurred.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During a project review, the sponsor asks for an overview of the project's current risks and how each is being managed. Which document should the project manager present?
o: The business case
The product breakdown structure
The project schedule
The risk register
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk register is the central record of identified risks, their assessed severity, planned responses and current status, making it the correct document for reviewing how risks are being managed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does effective risk management support communication within a project?
o: It removes the need to hold regular project team meetings
It removes the need to hold a contingency budget in reserve
It gives the team a shared understanding of potential challenges and responses
It allows difficult decisions to be deferred until project closure
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management aligns the team around known uncertainties and agreed responses, supporting open and transparent communication.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is an example of the risk response known as avoidance?
o: Removing a high-risk feature from the project's scope entirely
Accepting the possibility of a small delay to final delivery
Buying insurance to cover possible damage to project equipment
Increasing the budget to cope with late supplier deliveries
Risk & Issue Management.w: Avoidance removes the threat completely, for example by taking the risky element out of scope.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is NOT typically part of the issue management process?
o: Scoring the issue’s probability and impact
Closing the issue after resolution
Logging the issue in a formal register
Assigning an owner to the issue
Monitoring resolution progress
Risk & Issue Management.w: Scoring likelihood and impact is part of risk management, not issue management — issues have already occurred.

n.2: Issues are logged formally for tracking and resolution.
n.3: Each issue should have an owner responsible for action.
n.4: Progress tracking ensures resolution is followed through.
n.1: Formal closure confirms the issue has been resolved.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A high-impact risk was reduced by early action, and the manager records this in the register. Why does this matter?
o: It automatically triggers a review of the team's performance
It provides an audit trail of the risk treatment actions taken
It ensures the stakeholder matrix is kept fully up to date
It activates a formal contract change notice with suppliers
Risk & Issue Management.w: Recording responses and their outcomes in the register provides transparency and an audit trail that supports future learning.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the main objective of risk analysis in project management?
o: To approve outstanding change requests more quickly
To assess the likelihood and impact of each identified risk
To transfer every identified risk to external suppliers
To remove all uncertainty from the project's plans
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk analysis evaluates how likely each identified risk is to occur and how much it would affect the project's objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is normally the first step in a typical issue resolution process?
o: Escalating the issue directly to the project board
Closing the issue as soon as it has been recorded
Implementing a resolution before any assessment is made
Identifying and logging the issue in the issue register
Risk & Issue Management.w: The issue must first be identified and formally logged so that it can then be assessed, owned and tracked to resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following would NOT be classed as a project risk?
o: Potential cost savings from adopting a new item of technology
Confirmed damage that has already occurred to a delivery vehicle
Expected delays caused by forthcoming changes in legislation
Possible supplier delays arising from future industrial action
Risk & Issue Management.w: A confirmed event that has already happened is a current issue, not an uncertain future event, so it is not a risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During testing, a defect is discovered that prevents the product from being deployed. How should this be classified?
o: As an issue, because it has occurred and must be resolved
As a risk, because it may affect deployment later
As a baseline, because it defines the tested product
As an assumption, because it was expected during testing
Risk & Issue Management.w: The defect has already occurred and is blocking deployment, so it is an issue that must be managed to resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager maintains a risk management process throughout delivery. What is this mainly intended to achieve?
o: Better-informed decisions by anticipating and managing uncertainty
The removal of any need for quality management
A permanent record of every completed project activity
A reduction in the total number of project stakeholders
Risk & Issue Management.w: Ongoing risk management supports informed decision-making by anticipating uncertainty and planning responses.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What characteristic must an event have before it can be classed as a project risk?
o: It must be uncertain and capable of affecting the project's objectives
It must lie entirely outside the project team's ability to control
It must occur only during the execution phase of the project
It must be guaranteed to happen at some point during the project
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk must be uncertain and able to affect objectives, whether positively or negatively.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A product fails final testing because of a missed requirement, so the project manager formally records and recognises it. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Closure
Analysis
Identification
Resolution
Risk & Issue Management.w: Formally recording and recognising the issue is the identification stage, which begins the resolution process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier-capacity risk has been successfully dealt with through earlier delivery. What should the project manager do next?
o: Close the risk and record its outcome in the register
Leave the risk open in case the problem returns later
Remove the supplier from the project altogether
Escalate the risk to the project sponsor for a decision
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once a risk has been resolved it should be closed and its outcome documented to keep the register accurate.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the key difference in timing between issues and risks?
o: Both issues and risks relate only to events after project delivery
Risks relate to the future, whereas issues occur in the present or past
Both issues and risks are recorded only once lessons are learned
Issues relate to the future, whereas risks occur in the present or past
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks are anticipated future events, whereas issues are events that have already happened and are affecting the project.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A regulatory change that was once a major risk is now confirmed not to apply to the project. What should happen?
o: The risk should be re-analysed and given a new impact score
The risk should be formally closed in the risk register
The risk should be transferred to the project sponsor
The risk should be reprioritised as a high-impact risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: As the threat no longer applies, the risk should be formally closed and recorded in the register.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project's approval board is asked to decide how to resolve an issue affecting several workstreams. This situation best represents:
o: Issue escalation
Scope management
Risk reassessment
Stakeholder mapping
Risk & Issue Management.w: When an issue exceeds the project team's authority and is referred upward for a decision, this is issue escalation.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What takes place during the closure stage of the issue management process?
o: Assignment of ownership to a responsible person
Formal verification and sign-off that the issue is resolved
Implementation of the corrective action needed
Initial logging of the issue when it is first identified
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure confirms and records that the issue has been resolved, with the necessary verification and sign-off completed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A stakeholder demands that an issue be escalated before any assessment has been made. What should the project manager do?
o: Close the issue without recording any further detail
Assign the issue to a team member without logging it
Analyse the issue first to decide whether escalation is needed
Escalate the issue immediately as the stakeholder requests
Risk & Issue Management.w: The issue should be analysed first so the project manager can judge whether it genuinely exceeds project authority and warrants escalation.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager maintains a risk register and reviews it each week. How does this best support project success?
o: It removes all remaining assumptions from the project management plan
It allows risks to be monitored continuously and responses to be actioned
It ensures the lessons learned are all documented before work begins
It prevents any further change requests from being raised during delivery
Risk & Issue Management.w: Regular review of the risk register lets the team act on emerging threats and opportunities before they escalate.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During which stage would a project manager draw on lessons learned from earlier projects to spot potential risks?
o: Risk acceptance
Risk response
Risk closure
Risk identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: Lessons learned from previous projects are a useful input to risk identification, helping surface recurring or overlooked risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A possible delay to delivery is identified because a supplier may be overloaded with work. How should this be classified?
o: As a milestone, because it marks a delivery point
As a risk, because it has not yet happened
As a change request, because the plan must alter
As an issue, because it is affecting the project now
Risk & Issue Management.w: The delay is only a possibility that has not yet occurred, so it is an uncertain future event and is therefore a risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which action is most appropriate during the risk closure stage of the risk management process?
o: Reviewing the outcomes and updating the lessons learned
Increasing the project's contingency budget for reassurance
Converting each closed risk into a formal change request
Assigning new owners to risks that have already expired
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure involves recording outcomes and capturing lessons learned to improve risk handling on future projects.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does effective issue management benefit a project?
o: It helps maintain control and minimise disruption to delivery
It removes the need for a formal change control process
It guarantees that every deliverable will meet its specification
It eliminates all remaining risks from the project entirely
Risk & Issue Management.w: By recording and resolving problems promptly, issue management reduces their impact and helps keep the project under control.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project's main server crashes during a product launch. What should the project manager do first?
o: Replace the server without recording what happened
Log the issue and assess its impact on the project
Escalate the problem straight to the project sponsor
Cancel the launch until the server is restored
Risk & Issue Management.w: The first step is to formally log the issue and assess its impact so that an informed decision on the response can be made.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why are risks and issues typically tracked separately on a project?
o: Risk tracking is optional, whereas issue tracking is mandatory
Issues must always be resolved before the project can start
They follow different lifecycles and require different treatment
Only risks can be escalated to senior management for a decision
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks are analysed and planned for as uncertain future events, while issues are resolved as current problems, so they need separate processes and records.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A developer flags a design flaw that could delay testing if it is not addressed. How should this be managed?
o: Record it in the risk register, as it is a possible future event
Add it to the work breakdown structure as a new task
Escalate it immediately to the project sponsor for a decision
Record it in the issue register, as it has already occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: Because the delay has not yet happened and would only occur if the flaw is not addressed, it is an uncertain future event and belongs in the risk register.

Risk & Issue Management.q: At what point in the issue resolution process is ownership of the issue formally assigned?
o: During the analysis of the issue
Only if the issue is escalated
During the closure of the issue
Immediately after the issue has been logged
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once an issue has been identified and logged, ownership is promptly assigned so that resolution can be driven and tracked.

Quality.q: A quality control check finds that several components fail to meet the specification; what should happen next?
o: Ignore the failures because most components passed
Adjust the original scope to match the output
Change the requirements to suit the output
Report the failure and decide on corrective action
Quality.w: Non-conformance found in quality control should be reported so that corrective action can be taken to meet the standard.

Quality.q: Following project handover, who is normally accountable for tracking whether the intended benefits are actually realised?
o: The project sponsor or designated benefits owner
The finance administrator who managed the budget
The lead supplier who provided the deliverables
The project manager who led the delivery work
Quality.w: Benefits are usually realised after the project has closed, so accountability passes to the sponsor or a designated benefits owner identified in the business case.

Quality.q: In a linear life cycle, a board reviews whether the project should move into its next phase; what is this review called?
o: A stakeholder review
A decision gate
A post-project review
A formal quality audit
Quality.w: A decision gate is a review point used to decide whether a project should proceed to the next phase.

Quality.q: What is the primary purpose of quality control within a project?
o: To document the interests of the stakeholders
To confirm outputs conform to specifications through inspection
To produce a detailed and costed business case
To manage the contracts held with suppliers
Quality.w: Quality control verifies outputs through inspection, measurement and testing to confirm they meet requirements.

Quality.q: Which of the following would typically be discussed during a post-project review?
o: Lessons learned and performance against objectives
Plans for procuring brand new suppliers
Estimates for the costs of a new product
Detailed technical rework of the product
Quality.w: Post-project reviews cover overall performance, stakeholder feedback and lessons learned to inform future projects.

Quality.q: A construction project introduced quality procedures early and monitored them regularly; what benefit does this bring?
o: It removes the need to obtain stakeholder approval
It increases the likelihood that deliverables meet their specifications
It guarantees that no changes will occur during delivery
It reduces the amount of planning the team must do
Quality.w: Applying quality management consistently helps ensure deliverables meet agreed specifications and reduces the likelihood of rework.

Quality.q: A quality assurance review shows that a key process is not being applied consistently; what should happen next?
o: The findings should be ignored by the team
The project should be closed down immediately
Corrective actions should be identified and implemented
The product should be delivered without change
Quality.w: Quality assurance identifies process shortfalls so that corrective actions can realign work with quality standards.

Quality.q: A project has quality procedures in place but never reviews whether the team follows them; what is missing?
o: Risk management activity
Scope management activity
Issue control activity
Quality assurance of processes
Quality.w: Without checks to verify process adherence, quality assurance is not being properly implemented.

Quality.q: A benefit review finds that only part of the forecast savings were achieved; what should the organisation do?
o: Analyse why the benefits were not fully realised
Treat the whole project as a complete failure
Cancel all future benefit reviews entirely
Ignore the results because the project has closed
Quality.w: The gap between expected and actual benefits should be analysed and captured as lessons learned for future projects.

Quality.q: A manager arranges a peer review of the team's process to confirm agreed procedures are being followed; what is this an example of?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Scope verification activity
Change control process
Quality control of outputs
Quality.w: Quality assurance confirms that project processes are being followed correctly so that quality outputs are produced.

Quality.q: A team defines, plans and controls its processes so that outputs satisfy customer expectations; what is the purpose of this?
o: To provide the cheapest possible product to the customer
To shorten the overall project life cycle
To ensure deliverables meet stakeholder-defined standards
To transfer quality responsibility across to the suppliers
Quality.w: The purpose of quality management is to define the agreed quality requirements and ensure they are met throughout the project.

Quality.q: A project audit examines whether the team followed agreed processes. What is the main purpose of carrying one out?
o: To assess adherence to agreed policies, procedures and governance
To assign blame to individuals for the project's problems
To plan the scope of work for the next project phase
To approve the final invoice submitted by the suppliers
Quality.w: A project audit checks whether project activities have complied with internal and external standards and governance requirements.

Quality.q: A team inspects completed deliverables to confirm they meet the agreed requirements; which process are they performing?
o: Quality planning of outputs
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Stakeholder management work
Quality.w: Quality control involves inspecting and testing deliverables to verify they meet the agreed quality requirements.

Quality.q: During quality planning, a team agrees to follow recognised industry standards to guide development; what does this represent?
o: Selecting the quality measures for the project
Avoiding risk by outsourcing the work
Assigning the procurement roles for the team
Reducing project cost through standardisation
Quality.w: Choosing standards during quality planning helps define the measures used to verify that deliverables meet requirements.

Quality.q: A senior manager commissions a check on whether a project complies with corporate governance requirements. Which process is this?
o: Conducting a project audit
Planning the project's risk responses
Realising the project's benefits
Carrying out quality control
Quality.w: A project audit is the formal assessment of a project's compliance with governance, processes and policies.

Quality.q: Why is carrying out quality planning during the early stages of a project so important?
o: It guarantees the fastest possible project delivery
It removes the need to communicate with stakeholders
It reduces the budget the project will require
It defines how outputs will be verified against requirements
Quality.w: Quality planning establishes clear verification criteria, reducing rework and increasing confidence in delivery.

Quality.q: A sponsor asks how the team ensures their processes consistently produce quality outputs; which process is most relevant?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Procurement planning work
Quality control of outputs
Stakeholder analysis activity
Quality.w: Quality assurance focuses on the processes used to ensure that quality outputs are consistently produced.

Quality.q: A defect is discovered while the final product is being tested; which process is responsible for detecting it?
o: Change control process
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Issue resolution activity
Quality.w: Quality control detects defects through the inspection and testing of deliverables.

Quality.q: What is the main output produced by the quality planning process on a project?
o: A project closure report
A project risk register
A change control log
A quality management plan
Quality.w: The quality management plan sets out how quality will be defined, managed and verified throughout the project.

Quality.q: A project team is discussing whether their final product meets the definition of 'quality'. Which statement best defines quality?
o: Every project risk was successfully avoided during delivery
The final cost of the product came in below the initial budget
The deliverable includes as many additional features as possible
The output meets the defined requirements and serves its intended purpose
Quality.w: Quality means the deliverable satisfies its agreed specifications and is suitable for its intended use.
