Planning.q: A total cost is built up from detailed specifications and individual work package estimates. Which estimating method does this describe?
o: Analytical (bottom-up) estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
Planning.w: Analytical, or bottom-up, estimating aggregates detailed estimates from individual work packages to produce the overall figure.

Planning.q: A project manager is planning a new construction project. Who should be consulted to ensure operational handover requirements are captured in the plan?
o: The wider project team
The programme director
The end users
The project management office
Planning.w: End users define the operational needs that must be met for a successful handover into use.

Planning.q: During the early planning of a project with little detailed information, which estimating method is most appropriate?
o: Parametric estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Planning.w: Analogous estimating suits early planning, using high-level comparison with previous projects when detail is scarce.

Planning.q: Which estimating method is least effective when no historical data is available?
o: Analytical (bottom-up) estimating
Delphi (expert) technique
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
Planning.w: Parametric estimating requires reliable historical unit data to function, so it is least effective when no such data exists.

Planning.q: In which situation should analytical (bottom-up) estimating be preferred over analogous or parametric methods?
o: When only high-level assumptions are available
When detailed work package data is available
When an estimate is needed very quickly
When no historical data exists
Planning.w: Analytical estimating gives the most accurate result when detailed task and resource data at work package level is available.

Planning.q: In a linear life cycle the scope, timeline and budget are fixed at the start and rarely change. What does this indicate about the deployment baseline?
o: It changes on a daily basis
It is used only after the project closes
It is set early and used to manage performance
It is created during the benefits review
Planning.w: In a linear life cycle the deployment baseline is fixed early and used as a stable reference for controlling delivery.

Planning.q: At closure, a team wants to confirm whether the expected objectives and benefits have been achieved. Which element should they refer to?
o: The stakeholder matrix
The work breakdown structure
The success criteria agreed during initiation
The change control log
Planning.w: The success criteria agreed at initiation provide the benchmark for evaluating whether outcomes and benefits have been delivered.

Planning.q: A business case compares 'do nothing', 'do the minimum' and 'do something' approaches. Why is this comparison valuable?
o: It defines the criteria for project handover
It reduces the overall scope of the project
It demonstrates value for money and the case for change
It accelerates the procurement of suppliers
Planning.w: Comparing these options shows the value of proceeding and supports the strategic case for change.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Early feedback on a new IT system shows that users are confused by the interface wording. Which action best supports successful adoption?
o: Reassign the technical work to the users themselves
Transfer the concern to the sponsor as a risk
Arrange further end user engagement and training
Update the project governance plan
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Engaging and training end users after handover helps embed the solution and maximise the benefits realised.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A development team is waiting for its next batch of prioritised work. Who is responsible for keeping the backlog updated and correctly ordered?
o: The project manager
The product owner
The scrum master
The project sponsor
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The product owner maintains the backlog and ensures the most valuable items are ready for the team to develop.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: What distinguishes a project management office from a project manager?
o: The PMO provides oversight and tools across projects, while the manager delivers one project
The PMO reports to the project manager on each project by default
The PMO owns every work package, while the manager owns the schedule
The PMO leads stakeholder engagement, while the manager owns governance
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The PMO supports governance and consistency across projects, while the project manager is accountable for delivering a specific project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: An executive secured the funding and holds overall accountability for delivering the project's benefits. Which role is being described?
o: End user
Project manager
Project sponsor
Product owner
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project sponsor owns the business case, secures funding and is accountable for the realisation of the benefits.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following best describes the responsibility of a project team member?
o: Providing specialist skills and completing assigned tasks
Defining and owning the project business case
Approving transitions between project phases
Authorising procurement contracts with suppliers
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Team members apply their specialist skills to complete assigned work packages and report progress to the project manager.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: On a new IT project you gather requirements, attend progress meetings and support testing. Which role are you performing?
o: Project sponsor
Product owner
End user
Project team member
Roles & Responsibilities.w: A project team member completes assigned tasks and contributes specialist or technical input to the delivery of the project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A product owner postpones a planned feature so that a newly requested customer feature can be developed first. What does this decision demonstrate?
o: Formal change control escalation
Project risk avoidance
Backlog prioritisation and refinement
Project closure planning
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Reordering the backlog in response to customer value is a core product owner responsibility.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following would typically fall outside the responsibilities of the project manager?
o: Tracking and reporting project progress
Managing the day-to-day project risks
Approving strategic funding and benefits realisation
Leading the creation of the project schedule
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Approving funding and owning benefits realisation are sponsor responsibilities, not those of the project manager.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a key responsibility of the project sponsor?
o: Writing the detailed work breakdown structure
Maintaining the day-to-day project issue log
Producing the project communication plan
Approving key decisions and owning the business case
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor provides direction, owns the business case and approves the major decisions and investment for the project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a common responsibility of a project management office (PMO)?
o: Providing assurance and support across multiple projects
Owning and controlling the project budget
Managing the scope and deliverables of each project
Acting as the primary user of the deliverables
Roles & Responsibilities.w: A PMO offers governance, assurance, reporting and consistent support across projects or programmes.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A change in organisational strategy puts a project at risk of cancellation. Who is responsible for deciding whether it should continue?
o: Project sponsor
Project manager
Product owner
Project planner
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor assesses continued strategic alignment and has the authority to continue or cancel the project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best describes the difference between a product owner and a project sponsor?
o: The sponsor provides strategic oversight, while the product owner manages feature value
The product owner approves gateway reviews, while the sponsor delivers the outputs
The sponsor manages the backlog, while the product owner controls the funding
The product owner owns the business case, while the sponsor manages delivery tasks
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor secures funding and strategic alignment, whereas the product owner focuses on feature value and customer priorities.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A board has been assembled to oversee compliance, strategic fit and risk exposure ahead of a major investment decision. What role is it fulfilling?
o: Project management office
Product ownership
Project governance
Project team
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Project governance provides oversight, authorises decisions and ensures the project complies with agreed standards.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following would not typically be the responsibility of a project team member?
o: Providing progress updates to the project manager
Contributing specialist technical expertise
Delivering assigned tasks to the agreed specification
Tracking organisational benefits after handover
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Tracking benefits after handover is a sponsor responsibility, not part of a team member's delivery role.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following would not typically be a project governance responsibility?
o: Scheduling the team's day-to-day working meetings
Reviewing performance against project objectives
Providing strategic oversight of the project
Approving transitions between project phases
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Arranging routine team meetings is an operational matter for the project manager, not a governance function.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between the project sponsor and the project manager?
o: The sponsor sets direction and governance while the manager delivers
The sponsor manages daily delivery while the manager sets strategy
The two roles operate independently with no formal relationship
The sponsor handles finance while the manager makes technical choices
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor provides strategic direction and governance, while the project manager delivers the project within those boundaries.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A project manager needs a standard risk register template and guidance on preparing for a gateway review. Which role usually provides this support?
o: The scrum master
The project sponsor
The project governance board
The project management office (PMO)
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The PMO provides templates, tools, assurance and support to help projects plan and prepare for reviews.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A team member misses a critical deadline, affecting the schedule. What is the most appropriate response from the project manager?
o: Discuss the issue, find root causes and support recovery
Ignore it and quietly extend the project deadline
Assign the overdue task to the governance board
Escalate immediately to the sponsor for dismissal
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project manager should address the shortfall constructively, understanding the causes and working to recover the schedule.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: The sponsor has requested a progress report on the project. What should the project manager most appropriately include?
o: Updates on schedule, budget, risks and key deliverables
Strategic alignment assessments and funding approvals
Benefit realisation figures and post-project audit results
Detailed staffing contracts and future hiring plans
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Progress reporting communicates performance against schedule, budget, risks and deliverables so decisions can be made.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Warehouse staff who will operate a new inventory system daily are asked to test a prototype and give feedback. Which role are they performing?
o: Project manager
Project sponsor
Product owner
End users
Roles & Responsibilities.w: End users are the people who will work with the project's deliverables day to day and can give practical feedback.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: What is the primary responsibility of the product owner in an agile environment?
o: Producing the detailed technical documentation
Monitoring the delivery team's performance metrics
Prioritising the product backlog according to business value
Negotiating and managing the supplier contracts
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The product owner ensures the most valuable features are delivered by managing and prioritising the backlog.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A PMO introduces a lessons learned process across all completed projects. What is the primary benefit of doing this?
o: It identifies who to blame for previous project failures
It speeds up future procurement decisions
It supports continuous improvement across the project portfolio
It justifies staff changes within the delivery teams
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Capturing lessons learned helps future projects avoid repeat mistakes and adopt proven good practice.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A late supplier delivery has caused a critical delay. What is the most appropriate first action for the project manager?
o: Notify procurement that the project will be cancelled
Assess the impact and update the risk register and schedule
Escalate straight to the sponsor without any analysis
Reassign the whole project to the product owner
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project manager should first assess the impact and update the relevant records before recommending action or escalating.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Having approved the business case and committed funding, what should be a project sponsor's next priority?
o: Monitoring task-level performance of the team
Issuing procurement requests to suppliers
Developing the detailed project schedule
Ensuring strategic alignment and effective governance
Roles & Responsibilities.w: A key sponsor responsibility is keeping the project aligned to strategic objectives and supporting sound governance.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: In an agile project a stakeholder maintains the product backlog and decides which features are developed next. Which role is this person performing?
o: Project sponsor
Scrum master
Product owner
Project manager
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The product owner owns the backlog and maximises value by deciding the order in which features are delivered.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a core responsibility of the project manager?
o: Chairing the project steering group
Owning the business case and justifying the benefits
Authorising the release of project funding
Managing delivery against time, cost and quality
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project manager is responsible for delivering the project within the agreed constraints of time, cost and quality.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: You manage the day-to-day activities of a project, control its risks and ensure deliverables are completed on time. Which role are you performing?
o: Project team member
Project manager
Product owner
Project sponsor
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project manager runs the project day to day, managing time, cost, quality and coordination of the work.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is not normally a responsibility of an end user during a project?
o: Controlling the project budget and schedule
Taking part in user acceptance testing
Providing feedback on usability and functionality
Adopting the new system or process after handover
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Controlling budget and schedule is a project management responsibility and falls outside the end user's role.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A PMO analyst finds that three portfolio projects are reporting schedule delays and inconsistent risk data. What is the most appropriate PMO action?
o: Replace the affected project managers without delay
Compile the performance data and escalate the trends to governance
Cancel the three projects that are reporting delays
Take over delivery responsibility for the projects
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The PMO monitors and reports performance trends so that governance bodies can make informed decisions.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A developer finds that a technical constraint will prevent on-time delivery of a feature. What should they do next?
o: Raise the issue with the project manager and suggest options
Withdraw from the task and await reassignment
Notify the project sponsor of the problem directly
Escalate to the governance board for a decision
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Team members are expected to raise emerging issues with the project manager and collaborate on possible solutions.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following statements best describes the overall function of project governance?
o: Creating the detailed work breakdown structure
Running the daily stand-ups and team meetings
Ensuring strategic direction, decision-making and control
Maintaining the project's daily risk log
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Governance ensures the project stays aligned to strategy and follows agreed controls, decision-making and oversight.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Before handover is approved, the board requires confirmation that all deliverables meet the agreed scope and quality standards. What mechanism is this?
o: A risk escalation process
A work package authorisation
An issue log update
A decision gate review
Roles & Responsibilities.w: A decision gate lets governance confirm that agreed criteria are met before the project is authorised to proceed.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Staff using a newly delivered finance system report confusion over some features and ask for more training. What is the most appropriate project response?
o: Log the feedback and assess the options for supporting the users
Disregard the request because the project has already closed
Escalate the concern straight to the governance board
Amend the business case to add the requested features
Roles & Responsibilities.w: End user feedback should be acknowledged and addressed through support, training or further improvement to aid successful adoption.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A gateway review finds the deliverables no longer align with business strategy. Who is responsible for recommending that the project stops or is redirected?
o: Project governance board
Project team
Project manager
PMO administrator
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The governance board has the authority to intervene when a project no longer aligns to strategy or exceeds risk thresholds.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best describes the role of end users within a project?
o: They own the business case and ensure the benefits are realised
They define the strategic objectives and agreed scope of the project
They direct governance activities and approve the supplier contracts
They use the final product or service and give feedback during development
Roles & Responsibilities.w: End users interact with the deliverables and provide feedback that helps ensure the product or service is practical, usable and effective.

Communication.q: Which of the following is most likely to be included in a project communication plan?
o: A list of the sponsors of previous, unrelated projects
Escalation routes for unresolved communication issues
The individual salaries of the project team members
The technical hardware specifications of the deliverables
Communication.w: A communication plan commonly sets out how communication issues are escalated if they cannot be resolved.

Communication.q: What is a benefit of using email for communication on a project?
o: It is always a fully secure and completely private channel
It provides a written trail that can be referred to later
It functions without any need for an internet connection
It removes the need to hold project meetings altogether
Communication.w: Email creates an auditable written record that is easy to store and refer back to throughout the project.

Communication.q: What is a key benefit of summarising a verbal discussion in a follow-up email?
o: It guarantees the eventual success of the whole project
It removes the need for the original discussion to take place
It removes every possibility of the message being misread
It provides a record of what was agreed and the next steps
Communication.w: A written summary creates a record and reinforces shared understanding of what was agreed verbally.

Communication.q: What is a key limitation of using email as a communication method?
o: It is the most suitable channel for urgent decision-making
It is not actually a written form of communication
It lacks tone and non-verbal cues, so it can be misread
It always ensures an immediate two-way exchange of views
Communication.w: Emails can be misinterpreted because they carry no tone of voice or body language.

Communication.q: What is a downside of relying too heavily on informal verbal communication?
o: It guarantees that information is always communicated accurately
Agreements may go undocumented and be misunderstood later
It removes the need for any defined escalation routes
It substantially increases the volume of project documentation
Communication.w: Informal verbal communication relies on memory, so agreements can be forgotten or misunderstood unless confirmed in writing.

Communication.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of face-to-face communication on a project?
o: It removes any need for written follow-up or documentation
It reduces the travel and scheduling costs for the team
It permits immediate feedback and the reading of body language
It guarantees that stakeholders will agree with the message
Communication.w: Face-to-face communication conveys non-verbal cues and allows misunderstandings to be clarified immediately.

Communication.q: Why can face-to-face communication be less effective in certain project delivery environments?
o: It provides too much written documentation for the team
It can be impractical for dispersed teams or tight schedules
It excludes body language from the exchange of information
It removes the need to consider cultural sensitivities
Communication.w: For geographically dispersed or fast-moving projects, arranging in-person meetings can be costly and time-consuming.

Communication.q: What is regarded as the primary objective of communication within a project?
o: To remove the need for formal project documentation
To ensure that all identified project risks are mitigated
To support shared understanding among the project's stakeholders
To reduce the total number of meetings that are held
Communication.w: The purpose of communication is to ensure that everyone involved understands the relevant information and expectations.

Communication.q: A new stakeholder joins mid-delivery and the project manager uses the communication plan to brief them. Which benefit does this demonstrate?
o: A reduction in the number of technical defects found
Faster processing of change requests through governance
Improved oversight of supplier procurement activities
Consistent onboarding of stakeholders into established communications
Communication.w: The communication plan ensures new stakeholders quickly receive timely, relevant information and understand existing communication arrangements.

Communication.q: Under the communication plan, status updates are issued every Monday by 10 a.m. What does this help the project manager achieve?
o: Freedom from attending project governance meetings
Predictable updates that build stakeholder confidence
Automatic generation of procurement requests
The removal of any need to produce progress reports
Communication.w: Predictable, scheduled updates keep stakeholders informed and build confidence in how the project is being controlled.

Communication.q: Which of the following is a recognised disadvantage of video conferencing in projects?
o: Prolonged calls can cause fatigue and reduced concentration
It cannot be recorded for those unable to attend
It is always more effective than meeting in person
It guarantees that every participant contributes equally
Communication.w: Extended video calls can cause fatigue, which reduces attention and engagement.

Communication.q: External stakeholders report that they are not receiving relevant project information. Which document should the project manager review first?
o: The risk register's list of threats and their owners
The quality plan's checklists and acceptance criteria
The communication plan's stakeholder list and distribution schedule
The benefits register's expected outcomes and measures
Communication.w: The communication plan defines who should receive which information and when, so its stakeholder mapping and schedule are the first thing to check.

Communication.q: Which communication method best allows immediate two-way feedback and interpretation of tone and body language?
o: Posting to a shared online drive
Holding a face-to-face meeting
Distributing a printed newsletter
Exchanging threads of email
Communication.w: Face-to-face communication is the richest method, providing direct dialogue and non-verbal cues.

Communication.q: A communication plan states that weekly status reports go to the steering group, issued by the project coordinator. Which attributes does this define?
o: The audience, method, frequency and responsibility for the information
The probability, impact and response owner for a risk
The severity, priority and closure date for an issue
The supplier, contract value and delivery date for procurement
Communication.w: It specifies what is communicated, to whom, how often and by whom, all of which are standard contents of a communication plan.

Communication.q: What is a risk of stakeholders relying solely on written communication such as reports?
o: Reports are the ideal channel for resolving emotional conflict
Reports encourage immediate two-way dialogue between parties
Reports may be misinterpreted or ignored without discussion
Reports remove all ambiguity as soon as they are issued
Communication.w: Written reports can be overlooked or misunderstood, particularly where there is no chance to seek clarification.

Communication.q: What is a risk of overusing group email threads on a project?
o: They always deliver clear and unambiguous decisions
They can overwhelm recipients and dilute the key messages
They reduce the amount of information that is shared
They create an instant and reliable feedback loop
Communication.w: Excessive group emails can cause important information to be overlooked and reduce overall clarity.

Communication.q: In a fast-paced project with several stakeholder groups, what benefit does a communication plan provide?
o: It removes the need to carry out any risk management
It maps who needs what, keeping communication relevant and manageable
It guarantees that all communication happens in real time
It automatically prevents any changes to project scope
Communication.w: A good plan helps the project manager manage the volume and relevance of communication across diverse stakeholder groups.

Communication.q: What is a disadvantage of using physical noticeboards for communication on a project?
o: They provide real-time chat features for participants
They rely on people being present in person to see updates
They can be edited and updated remotely with ease
They automatically create a backup of their content
Communication.w: Physical noticeboards are static and only reach those who can access them in person.

Communication.q: A project holds a face-to-face kick-off meeting with key stakeholders. What is a genuine advantage of this approach?
o: It removes the need for any later follow-up communication
It lowers the travel and venue costs for the project
It speeds up the project's procurement decisions
It helps build trust and stronger relationships early on
Communication.w: Face-to-face interaction helps build relationships, trust and alignment at the start of a project.

Communication.q: Why is a communication plan especially valuable during stakeholder turnover or project handover?
o: It removes the need for any formal handover activity
It records prior communications, expectations and channels used
It allows new stakeholders to disregard past agreements
It prevents any future misunderstanding from ever occurring
Communication.w: A documented plan helps new stakeholders quickly understand the communication structures and the context of what has gone before.

Communication.q: What is a benefit of using several different communication methods on a project?
o: It removes the need to plan communication in advance
It reliably leads to information overload for stakeholders
It allows the project manager to reduce stakeholder engagement
Stakeholders receive information in the format that best suits them
Communication.w: Tailoring the method to each stakeholder's needs increases the likelihood that information is received and understood.

Communication.q: A stakeholder does not receive project updates because of a gap in the communication plan. What was most likely left out?
o: The earned value baseline agreed for the project
The storage location of the archived project data
The stakeholder's preferred method and required frequency
The project's formal change control process
Communication.w: A communication plan specifies who receives what information, when and how, so omitting these details can create gaps.

Communication.q: What is the benefit to the project manager of defining a communication frequency within the plan?
o: It ensures updates are delivered regularly and predictably
It guarantees that suppliers will meet their commitments
It allows decisions to be taken without any discussion
It removes the need to keep any project documentation
Communication.w: Scheduled updates create consistency and reduce ambiguity, helping to build stakeholder trust.

Communication.q: Before delivering a major milestone presentation, why would a project manager consult the communication plan?
o: To review the supplier's procurement performance
To approve an outstanding change request to scope
To confirm the audience, delivery method and timing of the update
To reassess the risk thresholds and escalation triggers
Communication.w: The communication plan defines the who, what, how and when of key information sharing, so it confirms how the milestone update should be delivered.

Communication.q: Which of the following is most likely to support effective communication on a project?
o: Delaying all project updates until the project reaches closure
Engaging stakeholders and delivering consistent, timely messages
Changing the communication approach at frequent intervals
Giving the delivery team only verbal instructions
Communication.w: Effective communication depends on engaging stakeholders and sharing consistent, timely information.

Communication.q: What is a key benefit of a communication plan to the project manager?
o: It prevents any conflict from arising within the team
It ensures consistent, structured messaging reaches the right people
It guarantees that the project will be delivered successfully
It removes the need to maintain any project documentation
Communication.w: A communication plan helps deliver the right message, to the right people, at the right time in a consistent format.

Communication.q: What is an advantage of using physical, paper-based communication in certain project environments?
o: It prevents any form of miscommunication from occurring
It gives a tangible, lasting record that does not depend on technology
It is always the quickest way to distribute project information
It guarantees that recipients will actually read the information
Communication.w: Physical communication provides a reliable, permanent record in environments where technology access is limited.

Communication.q: What is a common issue with relying solely on virtual communication platforms?
o: They are vulnerable to internet outages or system failures
They remove the need for any project documentation
They function without issue in every geographic region
They require no training for people to use them
Communication.w: Poor connectivity or system failures can disrupt communication entirely when it depends only on virtual platforms.

Communication.q: A manager defines communication as sending a message from sender to receiver 'with feedback'. Why is the feedback element important?
o: It confirms the receiver has received and understood the message
It formally records the message within the communication plan
It sets out the agreed scope for the project's deliverables
It introduces the technical terminology the team will use
Communication.w: Feedback confirms that the message has been received and understood, which is central to effective communication.

Communication.q: In which situation is a physical, printed communication method likely to be most beneficial?
o: When real-time collaborative editing is required
When rapid decisions must be reached within the team
When stakeholders are remote and rely on mobile devices
When working with non-digital audiences or in technology-restricted settings
Communication.w: Printed documents ensure accessibility where technology access is unreliable or absent.

Communication.q: Which of the following would you least expect to find within a project communication plan?
o: The format and frequency of routine status reports
A record of decisions already taken on the project
The preferred communication channel for each stakeholder
The individuals responsible for issuing project updates
Communication.w: A communication plan is a forward-looking tool; a record of decisions already taken belongs in a separate decision log.

Communication.q: Two departments received different updates and the sponsor asks why. How does the communication plan help the project manager respond?
o: It requires every department to receive identical content
It prevents the two departments from working together
It removes the manager's need to answer such questions
It records how communications were tailored and the reasons why
Communication.w: The plan documents who receives which information and why, allowing variations in the communication approach to be justified.

Communication.q: What benefit does a communication plan provide when conflict arises from misunderstood expectations?
o: It provides an agreed record of communication responsibilities
It guarantees that every team member is satisfied
It delays resolving the matter until project closure
It removes the need to involve stakeholders at all
Communication.w: Documented communication methods and responsibilities reduce ambiguity and provide a reference point that supports conflict resolution.

Communication.q: What is a major benefit of using virtual communication tools on a project?
o: They guarantee strong cohesion among all team members
They prevent technical problems from disrupting the project
They enable collaboration across different locations and time zones
They remove the need to engage with project stakeholders
Communication.w: Virtual communication allows geographically dispersed teams to collaborate effectively regardless of location.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help to reduce misunderstandings on a project?
o: By reducing the amount of stakeholder engagement needed
By clarifying who communicates what, when and how
By transferring all communication tasks to suppliers
By restricting the team to informal conversations only
Communication.w: Clear responsibilities and defined channels support accurate, consistent communication throughout the project.

Communication.q: What is a common disadvantage of relying on face-to-face communication in a project?
o: It can incur higher costs through travel and scheduling
It is too formal to be used in iterative environments
It limits the opportunities for participants to give feedback
It reduces the level of trust between team members
Communication.w: Although effective for building trust, face-to-face communication can be costly and time-consuming to arrange.

Communication.q: Which of the following best describes the typical contents of a project communication plan?
o: The system defects, their severity and current resolution status
The supplier contracts, payment terms and procurement schedule
The project's risks, their probabilities and planned responses
Stakeholders, communication methods, frequency and responsibilities
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who needs information, how and how often it will be provided, and who is responsible for providing it.

Communication.q: Why can virtual tools such as shared whiteboards be advantageous for collaborative planning?
o: They remove the need to keep any project documentation
They are inherently more secure than meeting in person
They prevent disagreement between the project's stakeholders
They allow asynchronous contributions from remote participants
Communication.w: Shared online tools support collaboration even when participants are not all available at the same time.

Communication.q: A project manager is drafting a communication plan. Which content should it include to ensure messages reach the right people?
o: The organisational charts of unrelated internal departments
The licence terms of the software used on the project
Stakeholders, methods, frequency and communication responsibilities
The catering preferences for the project's regular meetings
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who receives information, how and when it is shared, and who is responsible for sharing it.

Communication.q: What advantage does video conferencing offer when compared with a voice-only call?
o: It removes the possibility of any technical problems arising
It is more formal and removes the need for a meeting agenda
It guarantees that no message can ever be misinterpreted
It conveys visual cues such as facial expressions and gestures
Communication.w: Video adds non-verbal context to a conversation, helping to clarify tone and intent.

Communication.q: Which of the following statements best defines communication in the context of a project?
o: The process of completing and filing project documentation
A control activity used only during the planning phase
The exchange of information between people to reach shared understanding
The transfer of technical data solely to the project sponsor
Communication.w: Communication in projects is the exchange of information to achieve shared understanding and alignment among those involved.

Communication.q: Which of the following is a potential drawback of virtual communication methods?
o: They provide the same rich body-language cues as meeting in person
They remove every difficulty associated with differing time zones
They always ensure the confidentiality of shared information
They can suffer technical problems and reduced personal connection
Communication.w: Virtual tools can create barriers through technical limitations and weaker non-verbal engagement.

Communication.q: What is a limitation of relying on phone calls as the main communication method?
o: Calls always provide detailed visual aids for the discussion
Calls remove every risk of a message being misinterpreted
Calls may not be recorded or documented easily
Calls are always the best fit for project governance
Communication.w: Unless recorded or followed up in writing, phone calls can leave no official record of what was said.

Communication.q: Which communication method is most effective for detailed discussions that need clarification and negotiation?
o: Holding a face-to-face meeting
Issuing a monthly written status report
Sending a one-way recorded video message
Circulating a general group email
Communication.w: Face-to-face meetings allow complex points to be discussed and clarified immediately through two-way dialogue.

Communication.q: What is a benefit of using instant-messaging platforms within a project team?
o: They support fast, informal exchanges that aid quick decisions
They remove the need for the team to hold any meetings
They create a formal, legally binding record of decisions
They eliminate the difficulties caused by differing time zones
Communication.w: Instant messaging enables rapid, informal collaboration, which is useful for fast-moving issues.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help when several stakeholder groups with differing needs are involved?
o: It allows senior leadership to be left out of all updates
It restricts every communication to a single email channel
It requires the same message to be sent to every group
It lets the manager tailor messages to each audience's needs and influence
Communication.w: Communication plans support stakeholder-specific approaches, improving the relevance and effectiveness of engagement.

Communication.q: What is a major risk of using unstructured methods such as instant messaging for decisions?
o: They ensure the team complies with governance requirements
They leave no audit trail to trace how decisions were made
They improve the clarity of the project's agreed scope
They enforce formal stakeholder approval of every decision
Communication.w: Informal chats often bypass documentation, making it difficult to trace how and why decisions were taken.

Communication.q: A team uses a RACI matrix and a stakeholder register to inform its communication plan. What benefit does this bring?
o: Roles and responsibilities are reflected in tailored communication
The overall project schedule is noticeably shortened
Procurement is then able to proceed without any oversight
The need to carry out risk assessments is removed
Communication.w: Drawing on a RACI matrix and stakeholder register ensures each communication is directed to the right person in the most appropriate way.

Communication.q: What is a limitation of virtual communication methods when engaging project stakeholders?
o: It always guarantees full understanding of the message
It allows the physical handover of deliverables in person
It supports the same rich non-verbal cues as being present
It can reduce emotional connection and weaken rapport
Communication.w: Virtual settings can hinder relationship-building because of reduced physical presence and informal interaction.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What key benefit does effective scheduling provide to a project manager?
o: Improved levels of motivation across the project team
Easier negotiation with influential project stakeholders
Reduced financial risk within the project business case
Clarity on task dependencies and the overall project duration
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Scheduling makes dependencies visible and establishes how long the project will take, supporting sound planning and control.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of a project milestone?
o: To track the unresolved risks within the project
To assign specific tasks to individual project team members
To measure product quality against the baseline specification
To mark a significant point or achievement within the schedule
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones are zero-duration events that flag key points such as phase completions or major approvals within the schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Critical path analysis shows a task that can be delayed without affecting the overall project timeline. What is this an example of?
o: Float
Budget slippage
Configuration drift
Scope creep
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Float, or slack, is the amount of time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project's completion date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A team is given two weeks to complete as much as possible from a defined set of features. Which technique is being used?
o: Critical path calculation
Time boxing
Milestone tracking
Float analysis
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: This is time boxing: the duration is fixed at two weeks while the scope achieved within it is allowed to vary.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A schedule is revised to delay a task by three days so a shared specialist can finish another job first. Which technique is this?
o: Time boxing
Resource levelling
Resource smoothing
Risk transfer
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling resolves a resource conflict by moving task timings to match availability, even where this affects the schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a key benefit of agreeing a procurement strategy at the start of a project?
o: It removes the need to monitor suppliers once contracts are signed
It gives a structured, consistent approach to acquiring goods and services
It replaces the need to produce a business case for the project
It guarantees that internal resources are always selected in preference
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: An early procurement strategy provides a consistent, transparent framework for obtaining resources and services externally.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the main purpose of applying resource optimisation techniques when planning a project schedule?
o: To set the thresholds at which changes must be formally approved
To define how the project team will communicate with its stakeholders
To forecast how inflation will affect the overall project budget
To use resources efficiently and avoid periods of over- or under-allocation
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource optimisation adjusts the schedule so that resource demand is balanced, avoiding overloads and idle periods.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A team adjusts the start times of non-critical tasks to even out resource demand without delaying completion. Which technique is this?
o: Float analysis
Change control
Procurement scheduling
Resource smoothing
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing uses available float to reduce peaks in resource demand while keeping the project completion date unchanged.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project plan shows 'design approved' as a milestone. What does this most likely represent?
o: The list of resources assigned to the design work
The completion of a significant deliverable or decision point
The amount of effort required to produce the design
The total cost of the design phase of the project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone marks a significant achievement or decision point, such as an approval, rather than effort or cost.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is meant by the term 'time boxing' in project management?
o: Fixing the time allocated to an activity and allowing scope to vary within it
Assigning extra resources to the activities with the longest durations
Holding a reserve of unused time to draw on during emergencies
Extending the project deadline to accommodate additional scope changes
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing fixes the duration of an activity or phase, with the scope delivered varying to fit within the allotted time.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is identifying the critical path important to the success of a project?
o: It enables better control of time-sensitive tasks that affect the duration
It improves the project's overall stakeholder engagement strategy
It determines which procurement options the project will use
It ensures only the most skilled members are assigned to tasks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Knowing the critical path lets the project manager focus attention on the tasks that directly drive the completion date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When resource smoothing is applied and the project end date must not change, what typically happens to the schedule?
o: Non-critical tasks are rescheduled within their float to even out resource demand
All tasks are moved onto the critical path so delivery is faster
The scope of several tasks is reduced to lower overall resource demand
Additional staff are recruited so that the work can be shortened
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing keeps the end date fixed by rescheduling non-critical activities within their available float to level resource demand.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why might a project manager choose resource levelling rather than resource smoothing?
o: To reduce the number of stakeholders involved in the project
To remove the need for regular progress reporting during delivery
To keep the project's original end date fixed whatever the resource position
To resolve resource over-allocation even if the project end date must be extended
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling prioritises resolving resource over-allocation and may extend the schedule, unlike smoothing which protects the end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager finds that a key resource is assigned to several tasks on the same day. Which technique should resolve this?
o: Milestone tracking
Scope definition
Earned value analysis
Resource levelling
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling reschedules activities to resolve over-allocation, accepting that the end date may be affected.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In which type of project life cycle is time boxing most commonly applied?
o: Linear
Iterative or Agile
Extended
Sequential
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing is a core practice of iterative and Agile approaches, where time is fixed and the scope delivered is flexible.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the main purpose of a procurement strategy in project management?
o: To schedule the internal resources needed to complete project tasks
To identify and document the risks that face the project
To define how goods and services will be acquired from external suppliers
To assign roles and responsibilities to project team members
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy sets out how external products, services and resources will be obtained to support delivery.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a key difference between resource levelling and resource smoothing?
o: Levelling adjusts quality, whereas smoothing adjusts cost
Levelling may change the critical path, whereas smoothing does not
Levelling applies only to Agile, whereas smoothing applies to linear
Smoothing adds team members, whereas levelling removes them
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling can extend the schedule and alter the critical path, whereas smoothing works within float and preserves the end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of scheduling within a project?
o: To track the project's risks and open issues
To confirm that the business case is financially viable
To identify the key stakeholders of the project
To sequence activities and allocate time for their completion
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Scheduling sequences activities and assigns durations so the project can be planned and delivered within an agreed timeframe.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project needs a specialised system that only two suppliers can provide. What should guide the selection of a supplier?
o: The stakeholder communication plan
The lessons learned log
The project issue log
The procurement strategy
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The procurement strategy sets out the supplier selection criteria and contract preferences that inform such a decision.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following is a key outcome of performing critical path analysis?
o: A detailed quality assurance plan for deliverables
An understanding of which tasks have scheduling flexibility
A stakeholder influence and interest chart
A revised procurement contract for the main suppliers
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis distinguishes tasks with float from those without, showing where the schedule has flexibility.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a key advantage of using time boxing in project delivery?
o: It ensures delivery is prioritised within a fixed timeframe
It guarantees that the full scope will always be delivered
It removes the need for configuration management activities
It extends deadlines to allow further stakeholder approval
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Fixing the time forces prioritisation and focus, improving predictability of delivery within the agreed period.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A milestone marks the end of the testing phase. What typically happens once this milestone is achieved?
o: A completely new stakeholder engagement plan is produced
The project automatically moves straight into closure
The next phase of the project is authorised to begin
The project's risk register is permanently archived
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones frequently act as gates, confirming that work is complete and authorising the project to move into the next phase.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A sprint ends before all of its assigned tasks are finished. In a time-boxed approach, what happens next?
o: The team is formally penalised for missing the target
The sprint is extended until every task is complete
The incomplete tasks are permanently abandoned
The remaining work is re-prioritised for a future sprint
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing fixes the time, so unfinished work is reassessed and, if still needed, carried forward and re-prioritised.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager decides to buy in specialist development work from an outside supplier. Which document guides this approach?
o: The change request log
The risk register
The work breakdown structure
The procurement strategy
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The procurement strategy defines whether work is delivered internally or bought externally, and the criteria for doing so.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager uses a milestone to record the formal approval of the completed design phase. What does this milestone provide?
o: A checklist of quality requirements
An overview of team responsibilities
A schedule marker that shows progress
A register of the project stakeholders
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone marks a significant scheduled event, such as a phase completion or approval, providing a clear indicator of progress.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following would you typically expect to find within a procurement strategy?
o: Preferred contract types and the criteria for evaluating suppliers
The models used to support development of the project team
The amount of float available on each of the project's tasks
The categories used to prioritise the identified project risks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy defines how suppliers will be chosen, including preferred contract types and evaluation criteria.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the primary purpose of a milestone in a project schedule?
o: To mark the completion of a significant stage or deliverable
To calculate the total float available on the critical path
To allocate the project budget across its work packages
To record the daily effort logged by each team member
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone is a key point in the schedule, usually marking the completion of a significant deliverable or stage; it has zero duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A schedule shows that two activities must finish before testing can begin. What does this illustrate?
o: A task dependency
A work breakdown structure
A project benefits map
A scope verification check
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A dependency exists where one activity cannot start until another is complete; scheduling identifies these relationships.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the primary purpose of critical path analysis in project scheduling?
o: To identify the sequence of tasks that determines the project's duration
To define the overall scope of work for the project
To establish the stakeholder communication methods
To allocate team roles and responsibilities to members
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis identifies the longest chain of dependent tasks with zero float, which sets the minimum project duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why might a project manager include milestones within a project schedule?
o: To remove the need for a formal project management plan
To guarantee that the project finishes ahead of schedule
To provide clear checkpoints for monitoring and reporting progress
To increase the total number of activities shown on the plan
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones give recognisable checkpoints against which progress can be monitored and reported to stakeholders.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager prepares a Gantt chart to show when specific tasks will be carried out. Which aspect of scheduling does this support?
o: Financial and cost reporting
Task sequencing and time planning
Assignment of team roles
Identification of project risks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A Gantt chart is a scheduling tool that displays the order of tasks and when each is planned to take place.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager uses critical path analysis to find which tasks must finish on time to avoid delaying the project. What is being managed?
o: Critical path activities
The quality of project resources
The overall project budget
Formal stakeholder approval
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path activities have zero float, so they must be completed on time to prevent the project end date from slipping.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Your project is one of eight coordinated under a wider business change programme. What is the role of programme management here?
o: To coordinate and align related projects for greater benefit
To focus only on your project's budget and schedule
To monitor health and safety across the organisation
To take over the duties of the individual project sponsors
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Programme management coordinates and aligns related projects so they contribute to wider, shared business benefits.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A complex product must be delivered by combined IT and engineering teams. Which action best demonstrates project management?
o: Applying methods and tools to plan, execute and control delivery
Hiring additional administrative staff for routine services
Documenting every staff role across the whole organisation
Processing staff annual leave requests through a central team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Applying structured methods, processes and tools to plan and control the delivery is the essence of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Keeping a logistics project aligned to the sponsor's strategic vision is best described as an example of what?
o: One of the fundamental purposes of project management
A post-project review conducted after handover
A portfolio management responsibility above the project
A quality assurance activity carried out independently
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Ensuring the project stays aligned to organisational strategy and the sponsor's objectives is a core purpose of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why is the temporary nature of a project important to the way it is managed?
o: It ensures defined objectives are delivered within a bounded time frame
It removes the need for any stakeholder involvement during delivery
It guarantees the team can immediately be reused on other work
It aligns all delivery activity strictly to the financial year
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Being time-bounded focuses the project on achieving its specific objectives within defined constraints rather than continuing indefinitely.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: What is the key distinction between a programme and a portfolio?
o: A programme coordinates related projects; a portfolio oversees all projects and programmes
A programme contains only unrelated projects, while a portfolio does not
A programme is aligned to strategy, whereas a portfolio is not
A portfolio is always smaller in scale than a programme
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme manages a set of related projects, while a portfolio spans the organisation's entire collection of projects and programmes.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Suppliers across time zones face delays because responsibilities are unclear. Which core purpose of project management is being undermined?
o: Establishing a clear framework of control and governance
Removing the need for stakeholder input entirely
Delivering the final product without any change
Minimising all administrative overhead on the project
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A key purpose of project management is to provide clear control and governance, including defined roles and responsibilities for decision-making.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A finance team updates spreadsheets and processes invoices every day. How should this work most appropriately be classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves regular, repeatable tasks
Business-as-usual, because it has a sponsor and a budget
A project, because it is constrained by time and cost
A project, because it is carried out by a skilled team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Regular, repeatable work that maintains an ongoing service is business-as-usual, not a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is most characteristic of business-as-usual rather than of project work?
o: Producing a unique output using temporarily assigned resources
Delivering a defined scope within a fixed time frame
Delivering repetitive tasks and services on a continuous basis
Following a phased life cycle to achieve set objectives
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Business-as-usual maintains ongoing, repeatable services and functions, unlike the unique, time-bounded outputs of a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new data protection regulation takes effect during your design phase. Which analysis would help you understand its implications for the project?
o: A lessons-learned report
PESTLE analysis
A RAID log
Monte Carlo simulation
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE assesses how external legal and political factors, such as new regulation, may affect the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Several related projects are managed together to improve customer service and maximise value. What are they collectively part of?
o: A portfolio
A business case
A programme
A risk register
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to deliver benefits not available from managing them individually.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: What is the primary purpose of project management within an organisation?
o: To take over the responsibilities of programme management
To standardise every routine operational procedure in use
To provide a controlled framework for delivering unique objectives
To remove the need for any risk and issue management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management exists to provide structure, control and clarity so that defined, unique objectives are delivered.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: The board reviews every current project across IT, finance and HR to reallocate funding by business priority. What process is this?
o: Configuration management
Programme planning
Change control
Portfolio management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management provides strategic oversight, prioritisation and resource balancing across all of an organisation's initiatives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is not part of managing a project?
o: Identifying and managing project risks
Resolving issues that arise during delivery
Continuously delivering an ongoing business function
Communicating with project stakeholders
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management concerns temporary, defined outputs; the continuous delivery of a business function is business-as-usual, not project work.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A PMO balances resource allocation and risk exposure across a suite of unrelated IT and marketing projects. What is being demonstrated?
o: Operational management
Programme governance
Portfolio management
Project assurance
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Balancing investment, resources and risk across unrelated projects to serve organisational strategy is portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A charity is running a time-limited fundraising campaign. Why is managing it using project management principles appropriate?
o: Because the campaign forms part of routine operations
Because fundraising is a continuous, repeatable task
Because project management suits one-off, goal-focused initiatives
Because the campaign has no defined end point
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is designed for temporary initiatives with clear objectives and a defined end, which fits the campaign.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates work that would be classified as a project?
o: Answering routine user queries on a support helpdesk each day
Processing the organisation's payroll at the end of every month
Maintaining a client's existing software system throughout the year
Implementing a new customer relationship management system over six months
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A time-bounded initiative delivering a unique output, such as a new CRM system, is a project; the others are ongoing, repeatable business-as-usual tasks.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A sponsor wants ongoing visibility of progress and risk on a six-month IT upgrade. Which function of project management supports this?
o: Providing structured monitoring and control of delivery
Shifting the project's focus towards routine operations
Reducing the frequency of staff performance reviews
Allocating additional resources to business operations
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Structured monitoring, reporting and control of progress and risk are central functions of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A manager selects and prioritises all of an organisation's projects to align with strategy and balance resources. What are they managing?
o: A single workstream
A portfolio
A programme
A delivery team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management selects and prioritises projects and programmes across the organisation to meet its strategic objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which statement most accurately expresses the difference between a project and business-as-usual?
o: Business-as-usual has a defined end point, while projects continue indefinitely
Projects are delivered by a permanent team, while business-as-usual is not
Projects deliver defined change, while business-as-usual sustains current operations
Business-as-usual delivers unique outputs, while projects avoid any change
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Projects create change and specific deliverables, whereas business-as-usual keeps existing services running.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is most likely to be a portfolio management responsibility?
o: Selecting the right mix of projects to align with strategy
Ensuring two related projects are delivered in sync
Monitoring an individual project's risk register
Defining the detailed scope for a single project
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management ensures the right projects and programmes are chosen and prioritised to meet strategic goals.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: On a rural community project, high unemployment and low digital literacy threaten delivery. These are examples of which PESTLE factor?
o: Technological
Environmental
Political
Sociological
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Demographic and social conditions such as unemployment and literacy are sociological factors that affect adoption and delivery.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A general election is called midway through a public infrastructure project. Why would a PESTLE analysis be helpful in this situation?
o: It defines the contractual dispute resolution process
It identifies how political change could affect project governance
It calculates the project's critical path more precisely
It improves the breakdown of the technical design tasks
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE helps the project manager assess political factors, such as changes in leadership or policy, that may affect the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between project, programme and portfolio management?
o: Programme management replaces portfolio management in smaller organisations
Projects are managed independently of any portfolio or programme structure
Portfolio management provides strategic alignment, while programmes coordinate related change
There is no meaningful overlap between the three disciplines
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management aligns all projects and programmes to strategy, while programmes coordinate related change and projects deliver defined outputs.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A team reviews trends in renewable-energy legislation to see how they could shape a new facility's design. Which tool are they most likely using?
o: SWOT analysis
PESTLE analysis
MoSCoW prioritisation
Cost-benefit analysis
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE analysis identifies and assesses external factors, such as legislation, that could influence project outcomes.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why might a project manager carry out a PESTLE analysis during the initiation of a project?
o: To identify external factors that could influence the project
To map out the internal work breakdown structure
To set the payment schedule agreed with contractors
To evaluate the team's internal communication styles
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE analysis is used to identify external, macro-environmental factors that may affect the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following best explains the value of carrying out a PESTLE analysis at the start of a large project?
o: It helps anticipate external influences on the project's success
It defines the individual responsibilities within the team
It identifies the project's key delivery milestones
It estimates the cost baseline used for procurement
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE surfaces external threats and enablers early, helping the project anticipate factors beyond its direct control.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project is undertaken to deliver an output. How is that output most accurately described?
o: A permanent departmental responsibility
A sustained operational service function
A defined product, service or result
An adaptable ongoing support mechanism
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: APM describes a project's output as a defined product, service or result achieved within agreed constraints.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: You are delivering a new company intranet. Which of the following actions best reflects a project management activity?
o: Developing a risk register to manage delivery uncertainty
Running day-to-day maintenance on the existing intranet
Forwarding supplier invoices on to the procurement team
Producing the weekly staff timesheets for the HR team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Actively managing delivery risks is part of the structured, controlled approach that characterises project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A risk on a healthcare project is patient resistance to digital appointment systems. Which PESTLE category does this best fit?
o: Sociological
Economic
Technological
Legal
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Public attitudes and cultural acceptance of change fall under the sociological category of PESTLE.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: During an overseas product launch, the team flags that new tax legislation has been enacted. Which PESTLE category does this relate to?
o: Technological
Sociological
Environmental
Legal
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: New legislation, including tax law, falls under the legal category of PESTLE, which covers the laws and regulations affecting a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A company produces a one-off prototype for a client using a new design method. How is this effort correctly classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves routine manufacturing
A project, because it is a unique activity with defined outcomes
A project, because it forms part of regular production
Business-as-usual, because the client places orders frequently
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Creating a unique prototype with defined outputs is a time-bounded, one-off endeavour, which makes it a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following statements best describes what is meant by a 'project'?
o: A temporary endeavour undertaken to deliver a defined and unique output
An ongoing operation undertaken to sustain routine business functions
A continuous process undertaken to provide day-to-day customer support
A permanent department established to deliver repeatable services
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is a unique, transient endeavour with a defined beginning and end, undertaken to deliver specified objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a project?
o: An objective to deliver a unique output
A permanent team structure that continues indefinitely
A temporary nature, disbanding once objectives are met
A defined start point and a defined end point
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Projects are staffed by temporary teams assembled for the objective and disbanded on completion, so a permanent structure is not a project characteristic.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new appraisal system must be handed to HR within six weeks. What best distinguishes this project from HR's business-as-usual work?
o: The HR department holds greater control over the project budget
The project has a defined end date and delivers a unique output
The project exists to support HR's routine daily operations
The project is concerned only with engaging its stakeholders
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project delivers a one-off output within defined constraints and then closes, whereas HR's ongoing work is repeatable business-as-usual.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A sponsor is concerned that high inflation and rising interest rates could affect a capital investment project. Which PESTLE category applies?
o: Legal
Technological
Economic
Environmental
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Inflation and interest rates are economic factors, which directly influence a project's cost and viability.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A retailer runs related projects for online ordering, a mobile app and supply-chain automation. What ensures they are aligned for maximum benefit?
o: Programme management
Quality assurance
Change control
Portfolio management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Programme management coordinates related projects so their combined benefit exceeds what each project could achieve alone.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A city-centre event project faces growing scrutiny over its impact on local air quality and pollution. Which PESTLE category does this most relate to?
o: Technological
Environmental
Political
Legal
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Pollution, air quality and sustainability concerns fall under the environmental category of PESTLE.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following best summarises the key purpose of project management?
o: To take the place of business-as-usual activities
To help organisations deliver change and achieve specific objectives
To increase permanent headcount in operational areas
To standardise routine reporting across all departments
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management enables organisations to deliver change and meet specific time, cost and quality objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new CEO cancels two projects, starts three, and groups related initiatives into one programme. Which type of management is being applied?
o: Programme assurance
Change control
Portfolio management
Operational leadership
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Prioritising, terminating and initiating initiatives across the organisation to reflect strategy is portfolio management.

Life Cycles.q: A linear project has delivered and installed new equipment and has trained the staff who will operate it. Which phase is being completed?
o: Definition
Handover and closure
Concept
Development
Life Cycles.w: Handover and closure is where the deliverables are transitioned to the users and the project is formally brought to an end.

Life Cycles.q: A client wants a fixed upfront cost and schedule for deployment but also wants to evolve features after go-live. Which approach best fits?
o: Extended
Iterative
Hybrid
Linear
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid approach allows a predictable, planned deployment while retaining iterative flexibility to evolve features later.

Life Cycles.q: A team is building a new mobile app through short development cycles with regular end-user feedback. Which life cycle is most likely being used?
o: Extended
Hybrid
Iterative
Linear
Life Cycles.w: An iterative life cycle delivers in small increments and refines the product through repeated cycles of stakeholder feedback.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement best describes a core feature of an iterative project life cycle?
o: The full scope is fixed upfront and delivered in one release
Formal reviews are avoided throughout the delivery period
The product is released in increments with frequent reassessment
Benefits are only realised once the final delivery is complete
Life Cycles.w: Iterative life cycles release the product in successive increments, reassessing and adapting the plan after each one.

Life Cycles.q: Infrastructure is delivered using a linear model while customer-facing features are developed and adjusted during delivery. What is this model called?
o: Extended
Agile
Hybrid
Waterfall
Life Cycles.w: Mixing sequential and iterative components within one project is the defining characteristic of a hybrid life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: You are running a construction project with a linear life cycle and fully defined requirements. What is the correct sequence of phases?
o: Concept, Definition, Development, Handover and Closure
